explainer.one_liner: Oil and gas companies find crude and gas, ship it, cook crude into petrol, diesel, jet fuel and plastics, and sell it at the pump, the cylinder and the factory gate, mostly with the government looking over their shoulder.

doors.name: Upstream producers
doors.sub: Pump crude and gas from Indian fields and sell at a world-linked price, minus royalty, cess and whatever tax the government adds that year
doors.blurb: A bet on the crude price, net of the government's cut

doors.name: Refiners and marketers (OMCs)
doors.sub: Buy crude, refine it, and sell fuel at pumps whose price the government quietly steers
doors.blurb: A bet on crude falling while pump prices stay put

doors.name: Integrated private giant
doors.sub: One of the world's biggest refining and petrochemical sites, plus retail and telecom, funded by its own cash
doors.blurb: A bet on refining spreads, petchem spreads and the value of the businesses bolted on

doors.name: Gas and service tollkeepers
doors.sub: Earn a fee per unit handled: regasifying LNG, carrying gas or crude in a pipeline, renting a rig or a dive vessel
doors.blurb: A bet on volumes and contracts, not on the price of the molecule

explainer.door_analogy: Door one owns the farm and sells wheat at whatever the mandi pays. Door two runs the flour mill and the bakery, but the collector tells it what a loaf may cost. Door three owns the farm, the mill, the bakery and the mall. Door four owns the road and charges a toll on every truck.
explainer.door_so_what: The same crude price is good news behind one door and bad news behind the next, so you must decide which door you are buying before you look at Brent.

stations.name: Finding and pumping
stations.what: Crude and gas come out of wells; India pumps less than a sixth of the crude it burns and imports the rest
stations.who: ONGC, OIL, ANTELOPUS and Reliance's east-coast gas block at home; the Gulf, Russia, America and West Africa for the imported barrel

stations.name: Shipping and terminals
stations.what: Tankers bring crude and LNG to the west coast, where terminals unload, regasify and pipe it inland
stations.who: PETRONET at Dahej and Kochi, ENERGYINF's pipeline, the oil PSUs' crude pipelines

stations.name: Refining
stations.what: Crude is heated and split into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, LPG and naphtha
stations.who: RELIANCE at Jamnagar, IOC, BPCL, HINDPETRO, MRPL, CHENNPETRO, plus Nayara

stations.name: Petrochemicals and gas processing
stations.what: Naphtha and gas become polymers, polyester and fertiliser feedstock
stations.who: RELIANCE, IOC, ONGC's petchem arm, GAIL

stations.name: Pumps, cylinders and pipes
stations.what: Fuel reaches cars, kitchens and factories through petrol pumps, LPG dealers and city gas networks
stations.who: IOC, BPCL and HINDPETRO own most pumps; Jio-bp and Nayara the rest; city gas companies carry gas the last mile

kitchen.rival: OPEC+ and the Gulf refiners
kitchen.note: Jamnagar in Gujarat is the world's largest refining site and the west coast holds nearly all the LNG terminals, because that is where the tankers from the Gulf arrive. Pipelines then run east and north, which is why the eastern refineries pay more for their crude.
kitchen.so_what: India refines far more than it pumps, so the country is a margin business sitting on an imported raw material, and the dollar price of that raw material is the whole weather report.

end_markets.name: Road transport
end_markets.buys: Diesel and petrol, the bulk of every refinery's output
end_markets.moves_with: Freight activity, car and two-wheeler sales, pump prices

end_markets.name: Households
end_markets.buys: LPG cylinders and piped gas for cooking
end_markets.moves_with: Subsidy policy, cylinder price, city gas rollout

end_markets.name: Airlines
end_markets.buys: Jet fuel
end_markets.moves_with: Passenger traffic, airport capacity, the fuel tax states charge

end_markets.name: Fertiliser plants
end_markets.buys: Natural gas as feedstock for urea
end_markets.moves_with: Government gas allocation, urea subsidy, LNG spot price

end_markets.name: Power and industry
end_markets.buys: Gas, fuel oil and petcoke for furnaces and turbines
end_markets.moves_with: Gas price against coal, industrial output, pollution rules

end_markets.name: Plastics and textiles
end_markets.buys: Polymers, polyester chain and naphtha
end_markets.moves_with: Chinese petchem exports, packaging and garment demand

end_markets.name: Roads and construction
end_markets.buys: Bitumen
end_markets.moves_with: Highway building season, government road spending

end_markets.name: Export buyers
end_markets.buys: Diesel, jet fuel and petchem shipped from Jamnagar and the PSU coastal refineries
end_markets.moves_with: Global cracks, the EU's rules on fuel made from Russian crude, freight

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Diesel is the swing product: a weak freight quarter shows up in OMC volumes and in the diesel crack before it shows up anywhere else.

walk.input_label: Crude and gas bought, or levies paid on it

lines.why: Dollars earned per barrel between crude in and products out; the one number every refiner is judged on
What the pump keeps after buying the fuel from the refinery; set by politics, not by the market, and it swings from a loss to a windfall
A refinery holds weeks of crude, so a crude move marks that stock up or down and distorts a quarter in either direction
Refineries and fields are huge assets, but the charge is steady; it matters most in the years after a big expansion
Refinery expansions, new petchem crackers and offshore fields take five years and tens of thousands of crore; the cycle often turns before they fill
Crude in transit and government dues for LPG under-recoveries pile up on OMC balance sheets when crude spikes
OMCs borrow to fund both capex and unpaid under-recoveries; upstream and Petronet carry little debt
For upstream, the government's cut can take a large slice of every extra dollar of crude, so headline Brent is not what ONGC earns

pnl.analogy: A refiner is a dosa stall that buys batter at the world price and sells dosas at a price the municipality fixes. In a good month the batter gets cheaper and the dosa price stays, and the stall mints money. In a bad month it is the opposite, and the municipality promises to settle up later.
pnl.so_what: Strip out inventory gains before you judge a quarter, and read the marketing margin and the GRM separately, because one is a market and the other is a policy.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, in two opposite directions. Upstream earnings rise with crude, refiners and marketers earn most when crude falls while pump prices hold, and the tollkeepers barely notice. The cycle is tied to Brent, to refining spreads and to how much of the move the government lets reach the pump.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Demand returns after COVID-19, crude climbs, the Ukraine war sends diesel and jet cracks to records; upstream and Reliance earn fortunes

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Brent far above a hundred dollars; the government imposes a windfall tax on upstream and exports, pump prices are frozen and the OMCs post their worst losses in years

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Crude slides, cracks normalise, Chinese petchem capacity floods Asia; upstream realisations are capped by the tax while OMCs recover on frozen pumps

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Crude in the sixties, the windfall tax scrapped, LPG losses partly compensated; OMC marketing margins fat, upstream earnings thin

clock.position_detail: upstream wins, pumps frozen, OMCs squeezed

timeline.what: Crude in the sixties, OMC pump prices move daily, Reliance brings in Saudi Aramco talks for a stake in its oil-to-chemicals arm that never close.
COVID-19 empties the roads. Crude briefly trades below zero in America, Indian refineries run at two-thirds, and the government raises fuel excise to bank the fall rather than pass it on.
Demand roars back and Russia invades Ukraine. Diesel and jet cracks hit records, Reliance and upstream mint money, and India starts buying discounted Russian crude by the tanker-load.
The windfall tax arrives in the middle of 2022, pump prices are frozen, and the OMCs together lose heavily in one half-year, then recover as crude slides and the pumps stay frozen.
The best year in OMC history: crude in the eighties, pump prices unchanged, record marketing margins. A small pre-election price cut follows in early 2024.

Crude falls into the sixties, the windfall tax is scrapped, America slaps an extra tariff on India over Russian crude, and the government approves a compensation package for the OMCs' LPG losses. Upstream earnings sag.

Sanctions on Russian and Iranian barrels and the shadow fleet carry Brent back above a hundred dollars. Pump prices have not moved, so the OMCs are losing on diesel again while ONGC and Oil India enjoy the best realisation in years. The EU now bans fuel refined from Russian crude, and Reliance is preparing to list Jio.

hands.name: Brent crude
hands.meaning: Higher lifts upstream and squeezes OMC marketing margins; lower does the reverse

hands.name: Singapore refining margin
hands.meaning: Rising means every refinery earns more per barrel regardless of pump policy

hands.name: OMC marketing margin on diesel
hands.meaning: Turning positive without a pump price hike means crude has fallen enough to save the OMCs

hands.name: Russian crude discount and sanctions
hands.meaning: A wider discount is a gift to Indian refiners; sanctions that force a switch to Gulf crude cost margin

clock.so_what: At a crude peak the trade is upstream first and OMCs last, and it flips the day Brent breaks down, so hold the view on crude more tightly than the view on any company.

dials.name: Brent crude price
dials.channel: Realisation for upstream; input cost and inventory for refiners; marketing margin for pumps
dials.rise_does: lifts ONGC and OIL, squeezes the OMCs

dials.name: Singapore refining margin
dials.channel: The spread between crude and fuel products across Asia
dials.rise_does: lifts every refiner's profit per barrel

dials.name: Government pump-price policy
dials.channel: Whether crude moves are passed to the pump or absorbed by the OMCs
dials.rise_does: a hike restores OMC margins at once

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Every barrel is bought in dollars and sold in rupees
dials.rise_does: raises the import bill, widens OMC losses

dials.name: Sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil
dials.channel: The discount Indian refiners get on a third of their crude
dials.rise_does: removes the cheap barrel, raises crude cost

dials.name: Spot LNG price in Asia
dials.channel: Cost of imported gas for fertiliser, power and city gas; volumes at Petronet
dials.rise_does: cuts gas demand and regas volumes

dials.name: Windfall and other levies
dials.channel: The government's share of upstream and export profit
dials.rise_does: caps what upstream keeps of a crude rally

dials.name: Chinese petrochemical exports
dials.channel: Polymer and polyester prices across Asia
dials.rise_does: crushes Reliance's petchem spread

dials.name: Domestic fuel demand
dials.channel: Litres sold at pumps and cylinders delivered
dials.rise_does: lifts OMC and refiner volumes

dials.name: Ethanol blending and electric vehicles
dials.channel: Petrol displaced by ethanol and batteries
dials.rise_does: slowly shrinks petrol volumes

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track Brent and the Singapore refining margin; the first tells you which door is winning and the second tells you how much.

bottlenecks.name: Import dependence
bottlenecks.why: India imports more than four-fifths of its crude and about half its gas, so every geopolitical shock lands on the rupee, the current account and the refiners' crude bill at once.

bottlenecks.name: Government hand on the pump
bottlenecks.why: Petrol and diesel were decontrolled on paper years ago, yet pump prices freeze before elections and when crude spikes. The OMCs carry the loss and wait for a bailout.

bottlenecks.name: Windfall tax reflex
bottlenecks.why: When crude rallies the government has taxed upstream and export profit before, scrapping it when crude fell. The reflex caps upstream upside.

bottlenecks.name: Ageing fields
bottlenecks.why: Mumbai High and the Assam fields are decades old; ONGC spends heavily just to hold production flat, and new discoveries have been rare.

bottlenecks.name: LPG under-recoveries
bottlenecks.why: Cylinders are sold below cost to households, the OMCs book the gap, and compensation arrives late and partial.

bottlenecks.name: Sanctions and shipping
bottlenecks.why: A third of India's crude came from Russia at a discount; sanctions, tariffs and tanker insurance decide whether that discount survives each quarter.

bottlenecks.name: Petchem glut from China
bottlenecks.why: China has built more cracker capacity than it needs and exports the surplus, keeping polymer spreads thin for years at a time.

bottlenecks.name: Energy transition
bottlenecks.why: Ethanol blending, electric two-wheelers and gas-for-oil shift volumes slowly away from petrol; the refiners answer by pivoting to petchem and gas.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first three are the permanent shape of the sector and the reason OMCs trade cheaply, while the sanctions line is the live swing factor worth a daily look this year.

rulebook.body: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
rulebook.what: Sets policy, owns the PSUs and steers pump prices without a written rule
rulebook.why: A pump price hike or freeze is the single biggest OMC earnings event

rulebook.body: Directorate General of Hydrocarbons and the open acreage policy
rulebook.what: Auctions exploration blocks, polices production-sharing contracts
rulebook.why: Decides whether upstream can grow production or merely hold it

rulebook.what: Separates petroleum from mining law, lengthens leases, eases penalties
rulebook.why: Meant to bring in foreign explorers and stabilise upstream terms

rulebook.what: Regulates pipeline tariffs, city gas licences and open access
rulebook.why: Sets the toll that the gas tollkeepers earn

rulebook.what: Prices old-field gas as a slice of the crude price with a floor and ceiling, and gives deep-water gas a premium
rulebook.why: Decides ONGC and Oil India gas earnings, and the fertiliser and city gas input cost

rulebook.body: Special additional excise duty, the windfall tax
rulebook.what: A levy on crude production and fuel exports when prices spike, imposed in 2022 and scrapped at the end of 2024
rulebook.why: Could return if crude stays above a hundred; the first thing to read in any budget

rulebook.what: Taxes that make up a large part of the pump price
rulebook.why: Excise cuts are how the government shares crude relief; excise hikes are how it banks a crude fall

rulebook.body: EU ban on fuel refined from Russian crude
rulebook.what: Bars imports into Europe of diesel and jet made from Russian crude
rulebook.why: Indian exporters must prove their crude slate or lose a premium market

rulebook.what: Safety audits and clearances for refineries, terminals and offshore platforms
rulebook.why: An accident or a delayed clearance stops a plant

why.rivalry: Three PSUs own most pumps and price identically; upstream has two PSUs and the tollkeepers hold long contracts
why.supplier: Refiners buy crude from OPEC+ and sanctioned sellers at the world price; upstream's supplier is geology
why.buyer: The OMCs' real buyer is the government, which fixes what the public pays; gas buyers sign long take-or-pay contracts
why.entrants: A refinery costs tens of thousands of crore and a pump licence is slow; new entrants are rare and small
why.substitutes: Ethanol, electric vehicles and gas eat slowly at petrol and diesel; nothing replaces crude in petchem soon

forces.so_what: The tollkeepers keep the most profit per rupee of sales because they do not touch the price of the molecule; upstream keeps a lot when crude is high and the government is kind; the OMCs keep the least because their main customer is also their regulator.

cheat_sheet.metric: Gross refining margin, dollars per barrel
cheat_sheet.tells: What the refinery earned per barrel before anything else
cheat_sheet.good: Above $8/bbl for Reliance, above $6/bbl for the PSUs; compare to the Singapore benchmark

cheat_sheet.metric: Marketing margin per litre of diesel and petrol
cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the pump is subsidising the public or minting money
cheat_sheet.good: Positive on both fuels; ₹3–5/litre is a normal year, negative diesel is a loss year

cheat_sheet.tells: What ONGC and Oil India actually keep after discounts and levies
cheat_sheet.good: Tracking Brent within $3–5; a wider gap means a new levy

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether upstream is growing or just holding decline
cheat_sheet.good: Flat to rising year on year; a fall of more than 3% is a decline story

cheat_sheet.metric: EBITDA margin, stripped of inventory gains
cheat_sheet.tells: The underlying spread once the crude mark-to-market is removed
cheat_sheet.good: Refiners 6–10%, upstream 45%+, regas and pipelines 60%+

cheat_sheet.tells: How much of the capex and unpaid under-recovery sits on borrowed money
cheat_sheet.good: Below 2× for OMCs, below 1× for upstream

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the company is building the next cracker or field, or coasting
cheat_sheet.good: 1.5–2.5× while utilisation stays above 90%; above 3× is a watch

cheat_sheet.tells: Volume health for the tollkeepers
cheat_sheet.good: Above 90% at Dahej; a fall below 80% means spot LNG is too dear

lead_indicators.name: Brent and the Dubai crude benchmark
lead_indicators.channel: Inventory gains and upstream realisation move in the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: Singapore and Asian product cracks, weekly
lead_indicators.channel: Refining margins are a near-live read on the quarter

lead_indicators.name: OPEC+ output decisions and American shale rigs
lead_indicators.channel: Supply decisions today are crude price next quarter

lead_indicators.name: Sanctions news on Russia, Iran and the shadow fleet
lead_indicators.channel: Decides the discount on a third of India's crude a quarter ahead

lead_indicators.name: State and national election calendar
lead_indicators.channel: Pumps freeze before polls and sometimes thaw after

lead_indicators.name: Asian spot LNG price
lead_indicators.channel: Fertiliser and power switch away from gas when spot is dear, cutting regas volumes

lead_indicators.name: Chinese cracker start-ups and polymer prices
lead_indicators.channel: New Chinese capacity sets the petchem spread two quarters out

lead_indicators.name: Freight indices and vehicle sales
lead_indicators.channel: Diesel volumes follow trucks and petrol follows two-wheelers

rule.text: The OMC up-cycle starts when crude is falling, pump prices are holding and Singapore margins are firm; two of three means early recovery, and for upstream read the first sign the other way round.

call.headline: Crude at a sanctions-driven peak. Prefer upstream and the gas tollkeepers over the OMCs, and be ready to flip the day sanctions ease and Brent breaks.
points: With Brent above a hundred and pumps frozen, ONGC and Oil India earn the best realisation in years while IOC, BPCL and HPCL lose on every litre of diesel.
Petronet and the pipeline trust earn a fee per unit and barely notice the crude price, which is what you want when the direction is uncertain.
Reliance is a refining and petchem spread business with a telecom listing coming; the refining leg is fine, the petchem leg is still fighting Chinese oversupply.
would_change: Sanctions relief or an OPEC+ output rise that pushes Brent back toward the seventies
A return of the windfall tax on upstream, which would cap ONGC's upside
A pump price hike or an excise cut, which would end the OMC squeeze within a quarter

explainer.tell_a_friend: Oil and gas in India is one raw material and four different businesses. ONGC and Oil India pump crude and love a high price, though the government takes a slice whenever the price gets exciting. IOC, BPCL and HPCL buy crude, refine it and sell it at pumps whose price the government quietly fixes, so they make their best money when crude falls and the pump stays put, and lose money when crude spikes, as it has in 2026 on sanctions. Reliance does everything at Jamnagar and adds retail and telecom on top. Petronet and the pipeline trusts just charge a toll per unit and do not care what the molecule costs. In 2022 crude spiked, the OMCs bled and the taxman hit upstream. In FY24 crude fell, pumps held and the OMCs had their best year ever. Now crude is back above a hundred, so upstream wins and the OMCs wait for relief. Watch Brent, the Singapore refining margin and any news on pump prices or sanctions.

glossary.def: The North Sea crude benchmark most Indian crude contracts are priced off, quoted in dollars per barrel.
Finding and pumping oil; refining and selling it; and the pipes and terminals in between.
Oil marketing company: the three PSUs, IOC, BPCL and HPCL, that refine fuel and own most petrol pumps.
Dollars earned per barrel from selling products minus the cost of the crude. $8/bbl is a good year.
The benchmark refining margin for Asia, published daily; Indian refiners are judged against it.
The gap between the price of one product, say diesel, and crude. Diesel cracks drive Indian refiners most.
What a pump keeps per litre after buying fuel from the refinery and paying taxes. Set by how much the government lets the pump price move.
The loss an OMC books when it sells LPG or fuel below cost. The government may compensate it later, partly.
A refinery holds weeks of crude; when crude rises that stock is worth more and profit is flattered, and vice versa.
Special additional excise duty, a levy on crude production and fuel exports imposed in July 2022 when prices spiked and scrapped in December 2024.
Levies upstream pays the state and centre on every barrel produced, before income tax.
The crude price upstream actually receives after discounts and levies, in dollars per barrel.
The administered price for gas from old nominated fields, set monthly as a share of the crude price with a floor and a ceiling.
Open acreage licensing and the hydrocarbon exploration policy: the system where explorers pick their own blocks and bid for them.
Gas chilled into a liquid for shipping, then warmed back into gas at a terminal like Dahej for a fee per unit.
A contract where the buyer pays for the agreed volume whether or not it takes delivery. It is why Petronet's earnings are steady.
The Japan-Korea marker, the Asian spot price for a cargo of LNG. When it is high, Indian buyers switch to coal or cut gas use.
The oil-exporting cartel plus Russia, which decides output quotas and so steers the crude price.
Old tankers with murky ownership that carry sanctioned Russian and Iranian crude. Sanctions on them tighten supply to India.
How much cheaper Russian crude sells than Brent. Wider is better for Indian refiners.
The gap between a polymer's price and its naphtha or gas feedstock. Chinese oversupply has kept it thin.
A plant that breaks naphtha or ethane into ethylene and propylene, the building blocks of plastic.
The central tax on each litre of petrol and diesel; one of the biggest parts of the pump price.
Piped gas to homes and CNG to vehicles in a licensed area; the last mile of the gas chain.

explainer.one_liner: Cement companies dig limestone, bake it with coal or petcoke into clinker, grind it into grey powder, and truck it to the nearest house, road or bridge being built, because cement is too heavy to travel far.

doors.name: Pan-India majors
doors.sub: Plants in every region, national brands, the lowest cost per tonne and the power to set prices in a cluster
doors.blurb: A bet on consolidation: the big two groups buying the rest and prices behaving

doors.name: Regional players
doors.sub: One or two limestone clusters, a strong local brand, and whatever price the regional market allows
doors.blurb: A bet on one region's demand and price discipline, or on being bought out

doors.name: Value-added and blended specialists
doors.sub: White cement, wall putty and slag or fly-ash blends that sell for more or cost less to make
doors.blurb: A bet on a niche with its own pricing, sitting next to a grey cement business that behaves like everyone else's

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a national dairy brand with a plant in every state. Door two is the local dairy that owns the best cows in one district and sells in a few hundred kilometres. Door three sells paneer and ghee, which earn more than milk, but still has to sell milk too.
explainer.door_so_what: A regional stock is a bet on one cluster's prices, a major is a bet on the whole country plus the next acquisition, and the gap between them narrows every time a major buys a regional.

stations.name: Limestone mines
stations.what: Captive quarries next to the plant; a limestone lease is the licence to exist
stations.who: Every listed name on its own leases, auctioned by the states

stations.name: Fuel and power
stations.what: Kilns burn petcoke or coal at over a thousand degrees; power runs the mills
stations.who: Imported petcoke and coal, Coal India, captive power plants, waste-heat recovery and solar on site

stations.name: Clinker kilns
stations.what: Limestone becomes clinker, the hard grey nodule that is cement's active ingredient
stations.who: Integrated plants of ULTRACEMCO, AMBUJACEM, SHREECEM, DALBHARAT in the limestone belts of Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, the Deccan and Gujarat

stations.name: Grinding and blending
stations.what: Clinker is ground with gypsum, fly ash or slag into bagged cement, often at a unit near the city rather than the mine
stations.who: Split grinding units of the majors; JSWCEMENT and NUVOCO lean on slag; JKCEMENT on white cement

stations.name: Dealers and sites
stations.what: Bags go to retail dealers for homes, and bulk goes to builders, contractors and ready-mix plants
stations.who: Dealer networks of every brand; infra contractors and real-estate developers for the non-trade sale

kitchen.rival: Imported petcoke and coal (US Gulf, Indonesia, Australia)
kitchen.note: Limestone sits in a few belts, so plants cluster in Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Andhra and Telangana, Gujarat and Karnataka, and the cement then travels a few hundred kilometres by truck and rail. Freight and fuel each cost as much as the raw material itself, which is why the fight is for plants near demand, not for the best limestone.
kitchen.so_what: Cement is a local market dressed up as a national industry, so the price in Hyderabad and the price in Delhi can move in opposite directions in the same quarter.

end_markets.name: Individual home builders
end_markets.buys: Bagged cement through dealers, the largest single slice
end_markets.moves_with: Rural income, monsoon, housing subsidy schemes, bag prices

end_markets.name: Urban real estate
end_markets.buys: Bulk cement and ready-mix for apartments and offices
end_markets.moves_with: Home sales, launches, interest rates, developer cash

end_markets.name: Roads and highways
end_markets.buys: Bulk cement for concrete roads and bridges
end_markets.moves_with: Central and state road budgets, award pace, election years

end_markets.name: Railways, metros and ports
end_markets.buys: Bulk cement and sleepers, pre-cast
end_markets.moves_with: Government capital spending, project award cycles

end_markets.name: Irrigation and water
end_markets.buys: Cement for canals, dams and pipelines
end_markets.moves_with: State budgets, monsoon failures that trigger spending

end_markets.name: Industrial and warehousing
end_markets.buys: Cement for factories, data centres and logistics parks
end_markets.moves_with: Private capex, e-commerce, manufacturing incentives

end_markets.name: Government housing
end_markets.buys: Bags for affordable homes under central schemes
end_markets.moves_with: Scheme targets, fund release before elections

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Roughly two-thirds of cement goes into housing, so a strong infra budget cannot save a quarter when the home builder stays away, but a good monsoon and a rural recovery can.

lines.why: Profit per tonne of cement sold, the one number the whole sector is judged on; it doubles and halves across a cycle
The bag price after discounts; a few rupees a bag across millions of tonnes is the whole year's profit swing
Petcoke and coal are the largest cost and the most volatile; a fuel spike ate half the sector's margin in 2022
Trucks and rail cost almost as much as fuel; lead distance and diesel decide it
Plants last decades and the charge is steady, but a capacity race lifts it before the volumes arrive
A new integrated plant costs a lot per tonne and takes three years; the industry is adding capacity faster than demand and that caps utilisation
Dealers pay quickly and inventory is low; cement is a cash business
Low for the cash-rich majors, high for the acquirers and the regionals that borrowed to expand

pnl.analogy: A cement plant is a tandoor. The clay is cheap and sitting outside the door. The cost is the charcoal to keep it hot and the delivery boy to carry the naan while it is still warm. Profit is how much the neighbourhood is willing to pay for a naan this month.
pnl.so_what: Read EBITDA per tonne first and then split it into price, fuel and freight, because a margin rise built on cheap petcoke is borrowed and one built on price is earned.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, on two clocks at once. Demand follows housing and government capex, and margin follows the gap between bag prices and the price of petcoke, coal and diesel. Capacity additions run on a third, slower clock and decide how long any price rise lasts.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Post-COVID-19 cost cuts, firm prices and a housing revival push EBITDA per tonne to records; stocks re-rate

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Margins peak, every company announces capacity, Adani decides to enter by buying Ambuja and ACC

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Petcoke and coal prices double, then a price war as the big two chase market share; EBITDA per tonne roughly halves and prices fall to a multi-year low in 2024

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Election lull, weakest prices in five years, a wave of acquisitions of regional players; fuel costs fall, setting up the recovery

clock.position_detail: prices firm, fuel cheap, capacity racing

timeline.what: Demand slows with the economy and real estate; prices hold but volumes stall.
The COVID-19 lockdown empties plants for a quarter, then home building and cost cuts deliver record profit per tonne. The sector has its best margins ever.
Petcoke and imported coal prices double after the Ukraine war and margins collapse. Adani buys Ambuja and ACC and declares it will challenge UltraTech for the top spot.
Fuel costs ease and margins recover, but the capacity race begins in earnest: UltraTech and Adani both announce plans to reach far larger scale within a few years.

A price war. The majors chase volume, bag prices fall to the lowest in five years, elections stall government work. UltraTech buys India Cements, Adani buys Orient and Penna. Consolidation becomes the story.

Prices recover from the spring, fuel stays cheap, and the GST cut from twenty-eight to eighteen percent in September lowers the bag price for the home builder. JSW Cement lists. Demand turns up in the second half.

Early up-cycle. Housing and infra volumes are growing, prices are holding, and the big two groups hold around half the country's capacity. Shree Cement has just commissioned a grinding unit in the UAE. The risk is that capacity is still arriving faster than demand.

bottlenecks.name: Capacity outrunning demand
bottlenecks.why: The two biggest groups are racing each other to add plants, so national utilisation stays around seventy percent and any price rise invites a share grab.

bottlenecks.name: Fuel price swings
bottlenecks.why: Petcoke and imported coal are the largest cost and move with crude and freight; a spike takes two quarters to flow through inventory and cannot always be passed on.

bottlenecks.name: Freight and lead distance
bottlenecks.why: Cement cannot travel far profitably, so a plant in the wrong region is stuck with the wrong price; rail wagons are short in the busy season.

bottlenecks.name: Limestone leases
bottlenecks.why: New leases are auctioned by states and come with delays, royalties and local disputes; running out of limestone near an old plant is a real risk.

bottlenecks.name: Cartel scrutiny
bottlenecks.why: A few groups in each region set prices in step, and the competition regulator has fined the sector before and keeps watching.

bottlenecks.name: Monsoon quarter
bottlenecks.why: Sites stop in the rains, so the September quarter is always weak and often misread as a downturn.

bottlenecks.name: Carbon
bottlenecks.why: Cement is among the most carbon-heavy industries; India's carbon credit scheme and Europe's border tax put a price on the clinker, slowly.

bottlenecks.name: Election lull
bottlenecks.why: Government payments and project awards pause before polls, and labour goes home to vote.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The capacity race is the one that decides returns for the next few years; the rest are quarter-level noise that creates entry points if you can tell them apart.

rule.text: Cement is in an up-cycle when bag prices are rising, fuel costs are flat or falling, and demand is growing faster than capacity; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a false dawn.

call.headline: Early up-cycle with a capacity overhang. Prefer the low-cost majors and the regionals with new plants in tight regions; avoid paying for takeover hopes alone.
points: Volumes are growing on housing and infra, prices held through the GST cut, and fuel is cheap, so EBITDA per tonne is rising from the 2024 trough.
The big two groups hold about half of capacity and have bought most of the regionals worth buying, so price discipline should be better than in 2024.
The risk is the capacity pipeline: utilisation near seventy percent leaves room for another share grab if demand slips.
would_change: A petcoke and coal spike on the back of crude above a hundred dollars, which would hit margins by early 2027
A fresh price war led by one of the two majors chasing market share
A housing slowdown from higher rates or a weak monsoon

explainer.tell_a_friend: Cement is the most local heavy industry in India. Limestone is cheap and lies in a few belts, so the real costs are the fuel that bakes it and the trucks that carry it, and cement cannot travel far before freight eats the profit. That makes every region its own market with its own price. The whole sector is judged on one number, profit per tonne, which doubles when bag prices are firm and fuel is cheap and halves when fuel spikes or the big players start a price war. The last few years had both: a fuel shock in 2022 and a share war in 2024 that pushed prices to a five-year low, while UltraTech and Adani bought up regional players until two groups held about half the country's capacity. Now prices have recovered, fuel is cheap, the GST cut made bags cheaper and housing is building again. The worry is that new plants are still arriving faster than demand. Watch regional bag prices and the petcoke price; they tell you the quarter before the company does.

glossary.def: The hard grey nodule made by baking limestone in a kiln. Cement is ground clinker plus additives; clinker is the expensive part.
A plant that only grinds clinker into cement, usually near the market rather than the mine, to save freight.
A site with its own limestone mine, kiln and grinding mill.
Million tonnes per annum, the unit of cement capacity. India has over 650 MTPA installed.
Operating profit divided by tonnes sold. ₹1,000 a tonne is a good year, ₹600 is a bad one.
The average price actually received per tonne after discounts and freight adjustments.
Tonnes produced as a share of capacity. Above 75% producers can raise prices; below 65% they fight for volume.
Average kilometres a tonne travels from plant to buyer. Shorter is cheaper; above 400 km freight eats the margin.
Trade is bags sold through dealers to home builders at higher prices; non-trade is bulk sold to builders and infra at lower prices.
Petroleum coke, a refinery by-product burned in kilns. Cheaper than coal per unit of heat, priced off crude and freight.
Cement where part of the clinker is replaced with fly ash or slag. Cheaper and lower-carbon than ordinary Portland cement.
Share of clinker in a tonne of cement. Lower means more blending, lower cost and lower carbon.
Generating power from the hot gases leaving the kiln. Cuts the power bill and the carbon count.
A company's own power plant at the site, to avoid grid tariffs and outages.
The state-granted right to mine a limestone deposit, now awarded by auction, with royalty and a district mineral fund levy.
Higher-priced products for finishes and wall coating; a niche with better margins than grey cement.
Concrete mixed at a plant and delivered by truck to city sites; a bulk buyer of cement.
A period when the large groups cut prices to win volume. The one in 2024 pushed bag prices to a five-year low.
Big groups buying smaller producers. UltraTech and Adani did most of it in 2024-25.
India's emission-intensity market: plants that beat their target earn credits, plants that miss must buy them.
The EU's charge on the carbon in imported cement, steel and other goods.
The energy-efficiency scheme where plants get a target and trade certificates for over- or under-achievement.

explainer.one_liner: Steel companies melt iron ore with coking coal, or melt scrap with electricity, roll the hot metal into sheets, bars and pipes, and sell it to the people building cars, houses, bridges and machines.

doors.name: Integrated flat-steel majors
doors.sub: Blast furnaces fed by their own or bought iron ore and imported coking coal, selling hot-rolled coil, cold-rolled and coated sheet to autos, appliances and engineering
doors.blurb: A bet on the steel spread: coil price minus ore and coking coal

doors.name: Secondary and long-steel producers
doors.sub: Sponge iron, induction and electric furnaces making rebar, wire rod and billets for construction, often with captive power and pellets
doors.blurb: A bet on construction demand and on owning the raw material, especially iron ore

doors.name: Stainless and specialty
doors.sub: Stainless flat steel, alloy wire, ropes and recycled metals sold for what they do, not by the tonne of carbon steel
doors.blurb: A bet on a niche with its own price, though nickel and Chinese stainless still set the ceiling

doors.name: Pipes, tubes and wire converters
doors.sub: Buy coil or wire rod, shape it into pipes, tubes and wire, and charge a conversion margin on orders
doors.blurb: A bet on an order book from water, gas, oil and power projects, not on the steel price

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a big flour mill that buys wheat from the world market and sells flour by the sack. Door two is a local chakki that owns its own wheat field. Door three bakes cakes. Door four buys flour and makes biscuits to order for a hotel chain.
explainer.door_so_what: An integrated major is a bet on the global coil price and the coking coal bill, a secondary producer is a bet on construction and on its ore, and a converter is a bet on its order book, so the same steel price headline means different things for each.

stations.name: Iron ore and coal
stations.what: Iron ore is mined in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka; most coking coal comes by ship from Australia, with Russia rising
stations.who: NMDC, the state miners, captive mines of Tata Steel, SAIL and LLOYDSME; Australian coking coal

stations.name: Pellets and sponge iron
stations.what: Fine ore is rolled into pellets or turned into sponge iron with gas or thermal coal
stations.who: LLOYDSME, GPIL, SHYAMMETL, JINDALSTEL, plus many unlisted units

stations.name: Melting
stations.what: Blast furnaces or electric furnaces turn iron into liquid steel
stations.who: JSWSTEEL, TATASTEEL, SAIL, JINDALSTEL, NSLNISP, AM/NS India; secondary mills for longs

stations.name: Rolling and finishing
stations.what: Slabs and billets become coil, sheet, rebar, wire, pipe and stainless
stations.who: The majors' rolling mills, JSL for stainless, JINDALSAW, RATNAMANI, BANSALWIRE, USHAMART

stations.name: Users
stations.what: Builders, carmakers, appliance makers, railways and pipeline projects buy and use the steel
stations.who: Construction and infra contractors, autos, capital goods, oil and water utilities

kitchen.rival: China
kitchen.note: The steel belt runs through Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka because that is where the iron ore is; coking coal arrives at east-coast ports. China makes about half the world's steel and exports the surplus, so its export price is the ceiling on Indian coil.
kitchen.so_what: India is rich in ore and poor in coking coal, so an Australian coal spike or a Chinese export surge hits Indian spreads within a quarter.

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Construction and infra take well over half of Indian steel, so the government's capex budget matters more to volumes than the car cycle does.

lines.why: Profit per tonne shipped; the spread in one number, and it swings by half across a cycle
The biggest imported cost for blast furnaces, priced in dollars and swinging hard with Australian weather and Chinese demand
The domestic coil and rebar price after discounts; follows Chinese export prices with a lag
Large plants, steady charge; jumps when a new blast furnace starts
Every major is building capacity; a new blast furnace takes years and lots of borrowed money, and the cycle may turn before it fills
Coal and ore inventories swell when prices spike; converters carry receivables from government projects
Integrated majors carry heavy debt from expansions and acquisitions; debt to EBITDA decides who survives a bust

pnl.analogy: A steel mill is a mithai shop that buys sugar and milk at world prices and sells sweets at a price set by a giant shop next door, China. Some months the sugar is cheap and the neighbour is busy, and the shop prints money; other months the neighbour floods the street with cheap sweets.
pnl.so_what: Watch EBITDA per tonne against the coking coal price and the Chinese export price; the gap between the two is the next quarter's earnings.

clock.is_cyclical: Deeply. Steel profits follow the spread between steel prices and raw-material costs, and both are set mainly by China's construction cycle and its exports. India's own demand is the steadiest in the world, but it cannot set the price.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Global stimulus and China's restraint send coil prices to records; Indian majors earn their best margins ever and cut debt

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Coking coal spikes after the Ukraine war, the government imposes an export duty, and margins roll over

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: China's property crash pushes its surplus abroad at any price; Indian imports from China, Japan and Korea surge and coil prices fall to multi-year lows

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: A safeguard duty on flat imports puts a floor under prices; coking coal eases; margins begin to rebuild

clock.position_detail: duty floor, coal cheap, capacity rising

timeline.what: Slowdown. Auto and real-estate demand weak, prices fall, margins thin.
After the COVID-19 lockdown, stimulus around the world and Chinese restraint send coil prices to records. Indian mills earn record profit per tonne and pay down debt.
Coking coal more than doubles after the Ukraine war. The government slaps an export duty in May to cool domestic prices, then withdraws it in November. Margins fall from the top.

China's property crash leaves it with surplus steel that it exports at any price. Imports into India hit records and domestic coil falls to its lowest in years. Margins shrink even as Indian demand grows strongly.
A safeguard duty on flat steel imports arrives in April and prices firm. Coking coal is cheap. The majors push ahead with expansions and green-steel plans.

Early up-cycle. The safeguard duty is extended, Indian demand grows faster than any large economy, and the majors are adding capacity. China's exports remain the cap. The EU carbon border tax now charges on exports to Europe.

bottlenecks.name: Chinese overcapacity
bottlenecks.why: China makes about half the world's steel and its home demand is shrinking; the surplus goes abroad and caps prices everywhere.

bottlenecks.name: Coking coal dependence
bottlenecks.why: India has little good coking coal and imports most of it, so a shock in Queensland lands straight on Indian costs.

bottlenecks.name: Iron ore mining leases
bottlenecks.why: Leases expired and were auctioned in 2020, with high premiums to the state; owning ore is now a big advantage for a few names.

bottlenecks.name: Debt-funded capex
bottlenecks.why: Every major is building, and steel capex funded by debt has bankrupted Indian mills before, in the bust of the last decade.

bottlenecks.name: Policy swings
bottlenecks.why: The government has imposed export duties to cool prices and safeguard duties to protect them within a few years; either can move margins overnight.

bottlenecks.name: Carbon intensity
bottlenecks.why: Indian blast furnaces emit more carbon per tonne than most; Europe's border tax and India's own carbon market make that a cost line.

bottlenecks.name: Rail and port logistics
bottlenecks.why: Moving ore, coal and finished steel needs rakes and berths that run short in peak season.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: China and coking coal set the ceiling and the floor of margins, while policy swings and debt decide which company is still standing at the bottom of the cycle.

rule.text: Steel is in an up-cycle when Chinese export prices are rising, domestic spreads are widening over coking coal, and imports are falling; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a duty-propped rally.

call.headline: Early up-cycle behind a duty wall. Prefer names with their own iron ore and low debt, and the converters with long project order books, over debt-heavy pure blast-furnace growth.
points: Indian demand is growing faster than any large economy's, and the safeguard duty keeps Chinese steel at bay for now.
Captive ore is the biggest cost edge since the 2020 lease auctions, which is why the market pays up for ore-rich names.
Pipe and wire converters earn a conversion margin on orders, so they ride infra spending without betting on the coil price.
would_change: The safeguard duty lapsing or being cut while Chinese exports stay high
A coking coal spike from Australian supply problems
A slowdown in government capex after a budget squeeze

explainer.tell_a_friend: Steel is made by melting iron ore with coking coal in a blast furnace, or melting scrap and sponge iron with electricity. India has lots of ore but little good coking coal, so it imports the coal from Australia. The price of steel, though, is set by China, which makes about half the world's steel and dumps its surplus abroad when its own construction slows. So an Indian mill's profit is the gap between a Chinese-set price and an Australian-set cost. From 2020 to 2021 that gap was huge. In 2023 and 2024 China's property crash flooded the world with cheap steel and Indian margins shrank. In 2025 India put a safeguard duty on imports and prices firmed. Indian demand is the strongest of any big economy because of roads, railways and housing. The best-placed companies own their iron ore and do not carry too much debt. Watch the Chinese export price, the coking coal price and any news on the duty.

glossary.def: A plant that makes steel from iron ore through a blast furnace, then rolls it, all on one site.
A tall furnace where iron ore and coking coal react to make liquid iron.
Furnaces that melt scrap or sponge iron with electricity; cheaper to build and lower carbon.
Direct reduced iron: ore turned into iron with gas or thermal coal, without melting. Feeds electric furnaces.
Fine iron ore rolled into balls and baked so a furnace can use it.
A special grade of coal that turns into coke, the fuel and chemical agent in a blast furnace. India imports most of it.
The benchmark flat steel product, sold in big rolls; its price is the industry's headline price.
HRC rolled thinner and coated with zinc or paint for cars and appliances; earns a premium.
Ribbed steel bars that reinforce concrete in buildings and bridges; the main long product.
Flat is sheet and coil for autos and appliances; long is bars and sections for construction.
Operating profit divided by tonnes sold; the steel spread in one number.
Steel price minus the cost of ore and coking coal needed to make it.
Iron ore from the company's own mine, cheaper and more secure than buying it.
A temporary tariff on a surge of imports to protect domestic industry; India imposed one on flat steel in 2025.
A tariff on imports sold below fair price, after a DGTR investigation.
Directorate General of Trade Remedies, the body that investigates dumping and import surges.
Steel with chromium and often nickel, so it does not rust; priced partly off nickel.
Pipe made without a weld, for high-pressure oil, gas and boiler uses.
Steel made with much lower carbon emissions, through scrap, electric furnaces, gas or hydrogen.
The EU's carbon border tax, charging the carbon in imported steel from 2026.
Plants under construction, not yet earning or depreciating.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.

explainer.one_liner: Chemicals companies buy something cheap and messy from a refinery, a gas well, a salt pan or a mine, cook it in a reactor, and sell something purer to the people who make paint, medicine, pesticide, fabric and plastic.

doors.name: Commodity
doors.sub: Sold by the tonne; the world market sets the price; the company is a price taker
doors.blurb: A bet on a price you do not control

doors.name: Specialty
doors.sub: Sold for what it does, not what it weighs; two or three makers per molecule
doors.blurb: A bet on volume in a niche with some pricing power

doors.name: Contract manufacturing
doors.sub: You make a Western company's patented molecule for them, under a multi-year contract
doors.blurb: A bet on contracts: slow to win, slow to lose, and the stock falls hardest when one is lost

explainer.door_analogy: Door one sells rice by the sack at mandi price. Door two sells a spice mix people ask for by name. Door three is a chef cooking another restaurant's secret recipe under a long contract.
explainer.door_so_what: The first question for any name is which door it is behind, because a commodity name is a bet on a price, a specialty name on a niche, and a contract name on a customer.

stations.name: Ingredients
stations.what: Crude oil, natural gas, salt, sulphur, fluorspar, phosphate rock and power enter the kitchen
stations.who: Oil and gas PSUs, importers; China for fluorspar

stations.name: Refineries and crackers
stations.what: Crude becomes building blocks: benzene, ethylene, propylene, chlorine, caustic soda
stations.who: Reliance, the oil PSUs, GRASIM's chlor-alkali, chlor-alkali plants

stations.name: Intermediates
stations.what: Building blocks become hundreds of in-between molecules
stations.who: Indian listed makers in Gujarat and Maharashtra, with China at larger scale

stations.name: Actives and specialties
stations.what: Intermediates become the ingredient that does the job: a refrigerant gas, a crop-protection active, a pigment, a paint
stations.who: SRF, NAVINFLUOR, FLUOROCHEM, UPL, ASIANPAINT, PIDILITIND, HSCL

stations.name: Final product maker
stations.what: Paint, pesticide, medicine, fabric, pipe and fridge get made and sold
stations.who: Paint and adhesive brands, pharma companies, farmers, textile mills, auto makers

kitchen.rival: China
kitchen.note: Roughly half of India's chemical output comes out of Gujarat, around Dahej, Ankleshwar and Vapi, because that is where the port, the salt, the power and the effluent plants are. Geography is a cost line here.
kitchen.so_what: A shock at the first two stations lands straight on the margins at the middle two: when Reliance raises benzene or China cuts fluorspar, the listed names feel it a month later.

end_markets.name: Farming
end_markets.buys: Pesticide actives and intermediates, fertiliser
end_markets.moves_with: Monsoon, crop prices, farmer cash, global crop-protection inventories

end_markets.name: Pharma
end_markets.buys: Intermediates, key starting materials, solvents
end_markets.moves_with: Generic drug volumes, US drug-regulator approvals, China+1 sourcing

end_markets.name: Paints and coatings
end_markets.buys: Pigments, resins, titanium dioxide, solvents
end_markets.moves_with: Housing, repainting, auto production

end_markets.name: Textiles
end_markets.buys: Dyes and dye intermediates
end_markets.moves_with: Garment exports, cotton prices

end_markets.name: Plastics and construction
end_markets.buys: PVC, caustic soda, additives, adhesives
end_markets.moves_with: Real estate, pipes, government water schemes

end_markets.name: Auto and cooling
end_markets.buys: Refrigerant gases, polymers, fluids
end_markets.moves_with: Car and air-conditioner sales, Kigali gas quotas

end_markets.name: FMCG and personal care
end_markets.buys: Surfactants, flavours, oleochemicals
end_markets.moves_with: Rural consumption, palm oil price

end_markets.name: Electronics and energy
end_markets.buys: Fluoropolymers, battery and solar chemicals, industrial gases
end_markets.moves_with: Electric-vehicle and solar build-out

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Demand here is borrowed demand: a weak paints quarter or a crop-protection customer destocking is a chemicals earnings signal one quarter early.

lines.why: Selling price minus raw material; it tells you the state of the cycle before anything else does
Plants are expensive and depreciate from day one, but a new plant takes two to three years to fill, so margins fall while the future improves
Sales per rupee of plant; Indian specialty plants turn their assets at roughly half the rate of Chinese ones, which is the China problem in one number
Exports mean long receivables and inventory of a quarter or more is normal; customer destocking shows up here first
A small share of sales for most doors, but more than half the cost in chlor-alkali, where it is the whole story
Matters only in a build phase or for a leveraged commodity name
Nothing sector-specific

pnl.analogy: A chemicals company is a dhaba whose profit depends almost entirely on the gap between the price of a thali and the price of atta and dal. The cook's salary and the gas cylinder matter, but the gap decides the year.
pnl.so_what: Read capital work in progress and the capex-to-depreciation ratio together: well above one means building, near one means coasting, and a builder with falling margins is often the better buy.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes. Commodity chemicals move with price and specialty moves with customer inventories, and on top of both sits a slow structural tailwind, the world's wish to buy less from China.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Covid snarls supply, China rations factory power, then the Europe gas crisis makes European plants uneconomic; Indian spreads fatten and stocks re-rate

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Customers over-order for fear of shortages and every company announces capex

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Warehouses are full, Chinese capacity built in the boom comes online and exports at any price; product prices fall by a third to a half and stocks halve

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Destocking ends, volumes return but prices do not; anti-dumping duties are extended and Europe closes capacity for good

clock.position_detail: volumes back, prices capped

timeline.what: China shuts polluting plants. Indian chemical prices firm up and the China+1 story is born.

Covid snarls supply, China rations power to its factories, then the Europe gas crisis makes European plants uneconomic. Indian makers sell everything at fat spreads; specialty margins touch the high twenties and stocks trade at forty to fifty times earnings.
The peak. Everyone orders too much because they fear shortages, and everyone announces capex.

Customers find their warehouses full and stop ordering. Chinese capacity built during the boom comes online and China exports at any price. Many product prices fall by a third to a half, Indian gross margins shrink by several points and stocks halve.
The bottom. Destocking ends and volumes return, but prices do not. India extends anti-dumping duties and Europe closes capacity for good.

Early recovery, led by volume rather than price. Anti-dumping duty on phthalic anhydride extended, the duty on Chinese refrigerant gases recommended for extension, fresh anti-dumping probes on Chinese chemicals, and the Bhavya Rasayan scheme with dedicated chemical parks announced.

hands.name: Chinese chemical export prices
hands.meaning: Rising means the cycle is turning up for real; falling means China is dumping again

hands.name: Indian gross margins, quarter on quarter
hands.meaning: Expanding means the spread is back

hands.name: Inventory days at makers and customers
hands.meaning: Falling means the destocking is over

hands.name: Capex to depreciation with asset turns
hands.meaning: Both rising is a healthy build; capex up with turns down is how the next bust starts

clock.so_what: Early up-cycle rewards volume businesses first and price businesses last, so commodity names need Chinese prices to turn before they re-rate.

dials.name: China producer and export prices
dials.channel: The ceiling on every Indian price
dials.rise_does: lifts the ceiling on Indian prices

dials.name: European gas price
dials.channel: European competitors' cost
dials.rise_does: sends orders from Europe to India

dials.name: Crude oil and benzene
dials.channel: Raw material cost and product price, with a lag
dials.rise_does: squeezes spread for a quarter, then passes through

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Export earnings and the cost of imported intermediates
dials.rise_does: helps exporters, hurts importers

dials.name: Container freight and the Red Sea
dials.channel: Landed cost of Indian exports
dials.rise_does: hurts India more than China on Europe routes

dials.name: US tariffs on China
dials.channel: China+1 sourcing decisions
dials.rise_does: helps India if India is spared

dials.name: Monsoon and crop prices
dials.channel: Farm cash, so pesticide demand
dials.rise_does: lifts agrochem volumes two quarters later

dials.name: Interest rates
dials.channel: Capex funding, housing and paints
dials.rise_does: slows build-outs and the paints chain

dials.name: EU rules: REACH, PFAS limits, carbon border tax
dials.channel: Access to the European market
dials.rise_does: hurts fluorochemical exporters

dials.name: Kigali refrigerant phase-down
dials.channel: Quotas on HFC gases
dials.rise_does: turns a commodity gas into a licence

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track Chinese export prices and the European gas price; they explain most of the last seven years.

bottlenecks.name: China's cost advantage
bottlenecks.why: Scale, full integration from crude to active, cheaper power and patient state capital. India competes on niches, not on cost.

bottlenecks.name: Import dependence upstream
bottlenecks.why: India imports more than half its PVC, nearly all its methanol, most of its fluorspar and much of its phosphoric acid, so a supply shock upstream lands directly on Indian spreads.

bottlenecks.name: Environment and effluent
bottlenecks.why: Plant approvals take two to three years, the Gujarat pollution board can shut a cluster for weeks, and zero liquid discharge is a real capex line.

bottlenecks.name: Safety incidents
bottlenecks.why: Fires and explosions in Gujarat plants are a recurring headline and a recurring shutdown.

bottlenecks.name: Customer qualification time
bottlenecks.why: A contract customer takes two to three years to approve a plant. That protects incumbents and slows newcomers.

bottlenecks.name: Capital intensity
bottlenecks.why: The sector needs money before it earns money, so a rate cycle or a funding freeze stalls it.

bottlenecks.name: Agro seasonality
bottlenecks.why: Kharif and rabi sowing make agrochemical quarters lumpy, so a weak quarter is often the calendar, not the business.

bottlenecks.name: Hazardous logistics
bottlenecks.why: Ports, tankers and rail for hazardous cargo are scarce outside Gujarat.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two never go away and set the ceiling on returns; the next two are the surprise risks worth a news alert per company.

rulebook.what: Policy, incentive schemes and the new chemical parks
rulebook.why: The Bhavya Rasayan scheme and the dedicated parks sit here

rulebook.what: Investigates dumping and recommends duties
rulebook.why: A duty is a multi-year price floor for one product; watch its dockets

rulebook.what: Mandatory standards on imported chemicals
rulebook.why: Works like a tariff without being one

rulebook.body: CPCB and the state pollution boards
rulebook.what: Emissions, effluent and closure orders
rulebook.why: Shuts plants; the Gujarat board matters most

rulebook.what: Registers pesticides
rulebook.why: A registration is a moat for agrochem names

rulebook.what: Explosives and hazardous storage licences
rulebook.why: Licences gate capacity

rulebook.body: Montreal Protocol and Kigali, via the environment ministry
rulebook.what: Refrigerant gas quotas with an Indian freeze from 2028
rulebook.why: Converts refrigerants into a licensed business

rulebook.body: EU REACH, PFAS proposals, carbon border tax
rulebook.what: Access to the European market
rulebook.why: The next big external risk for fluorochemicals

rulebook.what: Inspects the pharma customers' plants
rulebook.why: A customer's warning letter is your lost order

why.rivalry: Commodity faces the world price, set by China; specialty has two or three makers per molecule
why.supplier: Few feedstock sellers in India and China controls fluorspar
why.buyer: Commodity buyers switch on price; contract buyers take years to qualify a plant and sign for years
why.entrants: Capital, approvals and know-how are barriers, but China is a permanent entrant into any commodity
why.substitutes: Regulators retire molecules: HFC to HFO gases, PFAS bans, pesticide bans; this hits specialty more than commodity

forces.so_what: Commodity keeps little of the profit, specialty keeps some and contract keeps the most, which is why the market pays the most for contract names and why a lost contract is the worst single headline in this sector.

cheat_sheet.tells: The state of the spread, so the state of the cycle
cheat_sheet.good: Expanding q/q; specialty above 45%, commodity above 25%

cheat_sheet.tells: Pricing power stripped of volume
cheat_sheet.good: Stable or rising; falling while volumes rise means a price war

cheat_sheet.good: Inventory under 100 days and falling

cheat_sheet.good: Exports 40%+ is fine; one customer above 25% is a risk

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the whole thing earns its cost of capital
cheat_sheet.good: Specialty 18%+ through a cycle, commodity 12%+

lead_indicators.name: DGTR dockets and duty extensions
lead_indicators.channel: A duty is a price floor from the day it is announced

lead_indicators.name: Gujarat pollution board closure orders
lead_indicators.channel: A closed cluster is lost volume the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: European gas price
lead_indicators.channel: Orders move at once, margins show a quarter later

lead_indicators.name: Destocking commentary from Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva and BASF
lead_indicators.channel: The customers' inventory is next quarter's order book

lead_indicators.name: Asian Paints and Berger volume commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Pigment and resin demand follows paint volumes

lead_indicators.name: Indian pharma and agrochem inventory days
lead_indicators.channel: Customers' stock falling means restocking next

lead_indicators.name: Chinese chemical export prices and producer prices
lead_indicators.channel: The price ceiling moves before Indian realisations do

lead_indicators.name: Monsoon progress and kharif sowing
lead_indicators.channel: Farm cash today is pesticide demand two quarters later

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when Chinese prices are rising, Indian gross margins are expanding, and capex is restarting with asset turns holding; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a false dawn.

call.headline: Early and uneven up-cycle. Prefer duty-protected and contract names over pure commodity until Chinese prices turn up.
points: Volumes are back but prices are capped by Chinese oversupply, so margins recover on volume first.
Duty protection is widening: phthalic anhydride extended, the refrigerant-gas duty recommended for extension, and fresh anti-dumping probes on Chinese chemicals.
The policy push, Bhavya Rasayan and dedicated chemical parks, is a slow tailwind for capacity, not a quarter-level one.
would_change: A fresh wave of Chinese capacity in a core product
A European gas price collapse that reopens European plants
An EU PFAS ruling that hits fluorochemicals

explainer.tell_a_friend: Chemical companies buy messy stuff from refineries and mines, cook it, and sell cleaner stuff to the people who make paint, medicine, pesticide and plastic. Their profit is one gap: selling price minus raw material. China sets the selling price for most of the world, so when China is weak and exporting cheap, Indian margins get squeezed, and when China cuts supply or Europe's gas gets expensive, Indian margins fatten. From 2020 to 2022 that gap was huge and the stocks went crazy. In 2023 and 2024 the gap collapsed and the stocks halved. Now volumes are back but prices are not, so it is early recovery. The companies that do best own a niche molecule or make someone else's secret recipe under a long contract. The ones that do worst sell by the tonne. Look at gross margin and new-plant asset turns, and watch Chinese export prices and the European gas price.

glossary.def: Selling price minus raw material cost. The sector's one big number.
Spread as a share of sales: sales minus raw materials, divided by sales.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: profit from running the plant, before paying for the plant or the loan.
The yearly charge that spreads a plant's cost over its life. It starts the day the plant opens, whether or not it is full.
Capital expenditure: money spent building or expanding plants.
Plants under construction, not yet depreciating. Tomorrow's capacity.
Sales per rupee of plant. 1.2 means ₹1.20 of yearly sales for every ₹1 of plant.
Money tied up in inventory and unpaid customer bills, minus unpaid supplier bills.
How many days of sales sit in stock. Rising means customers have stopped buying.
Customers running down their own stock instead of ordering. Orders fall even if end demand does not.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.
A seller who must accept the world price because its product is identical to everyone else's.
Making another company's molecule under contract: custom synthesis, or contract development and manufacturing.
Splitting salt water with electricity into caustic soda and chlorine. Power is half the cost.
The mineral all fluorine chemistry starts from. China mines most of it.
A tariff on imports sold below fair price. DGTR is the Indian body that investigates and recommends it.
A rule that an imported chemical must meet an Indian standard before it can be sold, which blocks cheap imports.
The global treaty phasing down HFC refrigerant gases. Each country gets a shrinking quota; India's freeze starts in 2028.
The EU's chemical registration rule: every substance sold in Europe must be registered with safety data.
Forever chemicals, a family that includes many fluoropolymers. The EU is considering broad limits.
An EU charge on the carbon in imported goods. Covers steel, cement, aluminium, fertiliser, electricity and hydrogen today, not organic chemicals.
The Dutch gas price that Europe's chemical plants pay. High gas makes Europe uneconomic.
The price factories sell at. China's chemical producer prices are the world's price ceiling.
Buyers adding a second supplier outside China, often in India.

explainer.one_liner: Mining companies dig coal, iron ore, bauxite, zinc and copper out of Indian ground, and either sell the rock as it is or melt it into metal, at prices set mostly in London or by the government.

doors.name: Coal miners
doors.sub: Sell most coal to power plants under long fuel-supply contracts at notified prices, and the rest through e-auctions at a premium
doors.blurb: A bet on power demand, e-auction premiums and a fat dividend

doors.name: Integrated base-metal majors
doors.sub: Own the mine and the smelter, sell zinc, aluminium, copper and silver at London Metal Exchange prices
doors.blurb: A bet on world metal prices against a cost base that sits in the lowest quarter of the global curve

doors.name: Iron ore and bulk miners
doors.sub: Sell lump and fines to steel mills at prices they post each month, tracking Chinese ore prices and Indian steel demand
doors.blurb: A bet on Indian steel output and on the government not taxing ore exports

doors.name: Processors and small miners
doors.sub: Turn ore or carbon into ferro alloys, graphite electrodes or refined copper, or trade minerals
doors.blurb: A bet on one product's price, often set by China, with thin protection when it falls

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the state milk cooperative: it sells most milk at a fixed price to schools and the surplus at the market. Door two owns the cows and the cheese factory and sells cheese at a world price. Door three sells raw milk to the local sweet shops. Door four buys milk and makes one specialty product that a big foreign brand undercuts when it likes.
explainer.door_so_what: Coal is a policy-priced dividend stock, the base-metal majors are a bet on London prices and their cost position, and the processors are leverage to a single Chinese-set price, so the same metal rally lifts them very differently.

stations.name: Exploration and leases
stations.what: The state finds deposits and auctions mining leases; the winner pays a share of revenue for decades
stations.who: Ministry of Mines, Geological Survey of India, state governments; COALINDIA and NMDC hold legacy leases

stations.name: Mining
stations.what: Open-cast and underground mines dig coal, ore, bauxite and zinc
stations.who: COALINDIA, BHARATCOAL, NMDC, HINDZINC, NATIONALUM, VEDL, SANDUMA, GMDCLTD

stations.name: Beneficiation and washing
stations.what: Raw rock is crushed, washed and concentrated to raise its grade
stations.who: The miners themselves, KIOCL for pellets, washeries of the coal companies

stations.name: Smelting and refining
stations.what: Concentrate and alumina become metal with huge amounts of electricity
stations.who: HINDZINC, VEDL, NATIONALUM, HINDALCO, HINDCOPPER, IMFA; China dominates the world's smelting

stations.name: Buyers
stations.what: Power plants, steel mills, galvanisers, cable makers and the export market take the output
stations.who: NTPC and state power utilities, steel majors, auto and electrical makers, global traders

kitchen.rival: China, for smelting and as the price-setting buyer
kitchen.note: The minerals sit in the eastern and central belt: coal in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh; iron ore in Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka; bauxite in Odisha; zinc in Rajasthan. Smelters follow the ore and cheap captive coal power, which is the main cost line.
kitchen.so_what: Owning a rich deposit plus cheap captive power puts Indian miners near the bottom of the world cost curve, so when prices rise most of the increase drops to profit.

end_markets.name: Power utilities
end_markets.buys: Thermal coal, the bulk of Coal India's output
end_markets.moves_with: Electricity demand, heatwaves, hydro and solar output

end_markets.name: Steel mills
end_markets.buys: Iron ore, coking coal, ferro alloys, graphite electrodes
end_markets.moves_with: Steel output, Chinese steel exports

end_markets.name: Construction and galvanising
end_markets.buys: Zinc for coating steel, aluminium for building
end_markets.moves_with: Infra and housing activity

end_markets.name: Power transmission and cables
end_markets.buys: Aluminium and copper conductors
end_markets.moves_with: Grid build-out, renewables, data centres

end_markets.buys: Aluminium sheet and cans, zinc and copper parts
end_markets.moves_with: Vehicle sales, beverage demand, electric vehicles

end_markets.moves_with: Industrial output, imported coal price

end_markets.moves_with: Solar installations, gold-silver prices

end_markets.buys: Aluminium, zinc, copper and iron ore pellets

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Coal follows Indian electricity and metals follow the world, so a heatwave helps Coal India while a Chinese slowdown hurts Hindustan Zinc, in the same quarter.

lines.why: For metals it is the London price plus premium, in rupees; for coal it is the notified price and the e-auction premium
Where the company sits on the world cost curve decides how much of a price rise it keeps
The biggest single cost at Coal India; a wage settlement every few years moves profit sharply
Smelting aluminium or zinc eats electricity; captive coal power is the main cost edge
Mines and smelters are long-lived; charges rise with new capacity
New smelters and mine expansions are lumpy and long; overruns show up years later
Power utilities pay Coal India late; metal inventories rise in weak markets
Low for the PSUs, heavy for the Vedanta group where parent debt drains dividends

pnl.analogy: A mine is a mango orchard. The tree costs the same to tend whatever the price of mangoes, so a good season price is nearly all profit and a bad one is nearly all loss. The best orchards are the ones with the cheapest water.
pnl.so_what: Read realisation and cost per tonne side by side every quarter; the gap is the earnings, and the cost line is the only part management controls.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes. Metal profits follow London prices, which follow China's demand, the dollar and supply shocks; coal follows Indian power demand and the imported coal price. On top sits the energy-transition story that is pushing up copper, aluminium and silver.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Stimulus, supply chains and the Ukraine war send metals and coal to records; e-auction premiums explode and miners pay huge dividends

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Aluminium and zinc peak early in the year; Europe's energy crisis shuts smelters; imported coal hits all-time highs

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: China slows, metal prices fall, e-auction premiums collapse and coal earnings normalise

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Metals stabilise, costs fall, and the market starts pricing the copper and silver shortage

clock.position_detail: copper, silver, aluminium high; coal flat

timeline.what: Weak metal prices, coal shortages at power plants, Coal India misses production targets.
COVID-19 lockdown crushes power and metal demand. Coal mining is opened to commercial private miners.
Metals soar on stimulus and supply chaos, then the Ukraine war sends coal and aluminium to records. A power crisis forces Coal India into record output and premiums.
China slows, metals fall and e-auction premiums collapse. Profits come off their peak.
Copper and silver climb on shortages, aluminium recovers, zinc steadies. Coal output crosses a billion tonnes and stockpiles pile up at power plants. Vedanta's demerger is approved.

A metals boom. Copper, silver and aluminium are near records on grid, electric-vehicle and data-centre demand. Coal is the laggard, with full stockpiles and weak premiums. The government is selling stakes and pushing critical-mineral auctions.

hands.name: Silver price
hands.meaning: Rising adds a large slice to Hindustan Zinc's profit

hands.name: Coal e-auction premium
hands.meaning: Rising premiums mean coal is short again; falling means plenty of supply

hands.name: Chinese industrial demand
hands.meaning: A Chinese stimulus would extend the metals boom; a slump would end it

clock.so_what: In a metals boom the base-metal majors print cash and the market prices the peak early, so the question is how long the copper and silver story lasts, not whether earnings are good.

bottlenecks.name: Leases and land
bottlenecks.why: Every new mine needs an auctioned lease, forest clearance and land from villages; projects slip for years.

bottlenecks.name: Chinese dominance
bottlenecks.why: China smelts most of the world's aluminium, zinc and copper and controls critical minerals, so its policy swings set prices.

bottlenecks.name: Coal transition
bottlenecks.why: Coal still runs most of India's power, but solar is growing fast; the long-run decline is real even if it is slow.

bottlenecks.name: Rail logistics
bottlenecks.why: Coal and ore move by rail; rake shortages in peak season strand output at the pithead.

bottlenecks.name: Group debt at Vedanta
bottlenecks.why: Parent debt pulls cash from listed subsidiaries through dividends and brand fees, a constant overhang.

bottlenecks.name: Wage and pension settlements
bottlenecks.why: Coal India's wage revisions come every few years and add a large one-time cost.

bottlenecks.name: State take
bottlenecks.why: Royalties, district mineral funds and possible export duties can grow when prices rise, capping upside.

bottlenecks.name: Monsoon
bottlenecks.why: Rains flood open-cast mines and slow despatch every September quarter.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: China and the London price set the cycle, but leases, rail and the state's cut decide how much of any boom an Indian miner actually banks.

rule.text: Mining is in an up-cycle when London metal prices are rising, Chinese demand is firming, and Indian power demand is strong; two of three means a partial boom, one of three means a narrow rally.

call.headline: Metals boom, coal flat. Prefer low-cost integrated metal majors with captive power and strong balance sheets; treat coal as a dividend holding, not a growth story.
points: Copper, silver and aluminium are near highs on grid, electric-vehicle and data-centre demand, and Indian majors sit low on the world cost curve.

explainer.tell_a_friend: Indian mining is really two businesses. Coal India digs most of the country's coal and sells it mostly to power plants at a price the government notifies, so it is a steady, high-dividend stock that moves with electricity demand. The metal companies, Hindustan Zinc, Vedanta, Hindalco and NALCO, dig ore, melt it with cheap power from their own coal plants and sell the metal at London prices. Their costs barely move, so when prices rise almost all of it becomes profit, and when prices fall it all disappears. Metal prices follow China, the dollar and supply shocks. In 2022 everything boomed, in 2023 it busted, and now copper, silver and aluminium are near records because the world needs them for power grids, electric vehicles and data centres. Coal is steady but not exciting, with full stockpiles. Watch London aluminium and copper prices, the silver price and India's power demand.
