explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a rice mill selling by the sack at mandi price. Door two is a branded basmati packet sold through kirana shops. Door three is the caterer who cooks for weddings on contract. Door four is a stall that got filed under rice by mistake.
explainer.door_so_what: A paper mill is a bet on a commodity price, a panel or laminate brand is a bet on home building and distribution, and a packaging converter is a bet on its customers' volumes, so check the door before you read a single number.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes. Paper follows global pulp prices and Asian import flows; panels follow the housing completion cycle and timber costs. Both had a boom after COVID-19 and a capacity-driven slowdown since.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Schools reopen, global pulp and paper prices spike, imports are scarce; Indian paper mills post record margins and panel demand surges with home upgrades

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Paper realisations peak, wood prices start climbing, every panel maker announces new MDF capacity

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Cheap paper imports from Indonesia and China, high wood costs and new MDF lines push margins down; paper stocks halve from the peak

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Imports stay heavy but quality rules on panels block some cheap supply; demand steady, margins thin but stabilising

clock.position_detail: margins thin, imports heavy, capacity filling

timeline.what: Steady paper demand, panel makers fight the unorganised sector after GST pushes some of it into the formal market.
COVID-19 shuts schools and offices; writing paper demand collapses for a year while packaging holds up.
Schools reopen, pulp prices spike, imports dry up. Paper mills earn record margins and home upgrades lift panel and laminate demand.
Pulp falls, cheap Asian paper floods in, wood costs climb. Panel makers all add MDF lines at once and price wars break out.
Quality control orders on plywood, MDF and particle board come into force, blocking some low-grade imports. Paper imports stay heavy. Margins stay thin.
Bottoming. Panel demand rises with housing completions, new MDF lines fill, and the industry asks for safeguard action on paper imports. Plastic bans keep the packaging story alive.

explainer.tell_a_friend: This bucket covers three real businesses. Paper mills like JK Paper turn farm-grown eucalyptus and bamboo into notebook paper and packaging board, but the price is set by cheap imports from Indonesia and China, so when imports flood in, margins shrink. Panel makers like Century, Greenply and Greenpanel turn wood into plywood, MDF and laminates, and sell through carpenters who ask for the brand, so they hold price better and follow home completions. Packaging converters turn board into printed cartons for FMCG brands. All of them depend on wood, which India grows too little of, so wood prices have stayed high since 2022. After a boom in 2021 and 2022, paper margins fell as imports returned, and panel makers all built MDF lines at once and started a price war. Now the new lines are filling, quality rules block some cheap panels, and housing completions are strong. Watch import prices, wood costs and MDF utilisation.

explainer.one_liner: Capital goods companies make the machines that make everything else: the transformers and switchgear that carry power, the boilers and turbines inside a plant, the engines, forgings and cables that go into factories, grids, railways and buildings.

doors.name: Grid and power equipment
doors.sub: Transformers, switchgear, motors, drives and automation sold product by product off a fat order book, mostly to utilities and factories
doors.blurb: A bet on the power-grid build-out and on a shortage of transformer capacity that keeps prices firm

doors.name: Project builders
doors.sub: Build a whole plant, line or refinery to order, paid in milestones over years; the margin is thin and the working capital is heavy
doors.blurb: A bet on government and PSU capex, and on executing without cost overruns

doors.name: Wires, cables and electricals
doors.sub: Copper and aluminium turned into cables, wires, fans and switches, sold through dealers and to projects; the metal price passes through
doors.blurb: A bet on volume growth and distribution reach, with copper as a quarterly nuisance

doors.name: Engines, forgings and explosives
doors.sub: Components and consumables sold into other people's machines and mines: gensets, crankshafts, industrial explosives
doors.blurb: A bet on factory, mining and now defence volumes, with export exposure to the US and Europe

explainer.door_analogy: Door one sells the sewing machines by the piece from a waiting list. Door two agrees to build the whole garment factory for a fixed price and hopes nothing goes wrong. Door three sells thread and buttons by the kilo, with the metal price written on the invoice. Door four sells the motors that go inside everyone else's machines.
explainer.door_so_what: An equipment maker lives off its order book and its margin, a project builder lives off execution and cash collection, and a cable maker lives off volume, so the same headline about capex means three different things.

stations.name: Project integration

stations.name: The buyer
stations.what: A utility, a PSU, a factory, a railway or a developer takes delivery and pays over years
stations.who: Power Grid, NTPC, state utilities, Indian Railways, refiners, data-centre and renewable developers

kitchen.rival: China
kitchen.note: The heavy electrical cluster sits around Vadodara, Bengaluru, Nashik and Bhopal, with components in Pune and Coimbatore. The one input India does not make at scale is electrical steel for transformer cores, so a transformer's cost line starts in Japan and Korea.
kitchen.so_what: The grid names at the third station are enjoying a seller's market because transformer capacity worldwide is short; the project builders at the fourth station are still price takers in a tender.

explainer.end_markets_so_what: The grid and renewables buyers are the ones ordering today; private factories are the swing buyer that would turn a good cycle into a great one, and they have not fully shown up.

lines.why: Not a P&L line, but the P&L of two years from now; the market reads it before anything else
Tells you whether a fixed-price order is still profitable after copper and steel moved
Project builders carry retention money, unbilled revenue and customer advances; a rising receivable number is the first sign of a stuck project
Asset-light for most doors, which is why return on capital is high; the exception is a transformer or electrical-steel capacity build
Small for assemblers and contractors; plants are cheap next to the sales they carry
Matters for leveraged project builders and for the cost of bank guarantees, not for cash-rich multinationals
Customer advances sit as cash and earn interest; a chunk of a project builder's profit can be treasury income
A single stuck fixed-price project can wipe out a year of margin, which is the project door's defining risk

pnl.analogy: An equipment maker is a tailor with a two-year waiting list who can raise prices because nobody else has a free sewing machine. A project builder is a caterer who quoted a fixed price for a wedding a year ago and is now watching the price of ghee.
pnl.so_what: Read order inflow against sales to see if the book is still growing, then read gross margin to see whether the book is worth having.

clock.is_cyclical: Deeply cyclical, and the cycle is long. It runs on government, utility and private capex, which moves in decade-long waves, with elections, interest rates and a shortage or glut of specific equipment on top.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Power plants, roads and private factories are ordered everywhere; order books triple and every stock is a multibagger

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Capacity is added at the top, Chinese boiler and turbine makers undercut on price and private power developers over-borrow

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Stranded power projects, bad bank loans and a decade of no private capex; BHEL's profit collapses and order books shrink for years

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Covid stops sites, orders are deferred and the sector trades as if capex will never return

clock.position_detail: grid orders strong, private capex lagging

timeline.what: The old capex drought. Private industry is not investing, the shadow-bank crisis freezes project finance and the sector is unloved.
Covid shuts construction sites and factories. The bottom. Government announces production-linked incentive schemes to pull manufacturing in.
Government capex rises sharply every budget, the railway and road pipelines fill, and the first big transmission tenders for renewable evacuation appear. Order inflows turn up.

The grid build-out becomes a global story. Transformer and switchgear capacity is short worldwide, delivery times stretch to years and the multinationals' Indian arms re-rate hard. Data centres join as a buyer.
Election year. Government order placement slows for two quarters, but the order books are already full and margins expand as old low-price orders roll off. Valuations hit highs.
Thermal power ordering revives after years, new transmission lines are awarded, US tariffs cloud exports for forging and engine names and private capex stays patchy.

Results confirm the earnings phase of the cycle: BHEL's quarterly profit more than doubles, transformer makers run at full utilisation, and grid investors call for stronger connections as power demand grows. The debate is valuation, not demand.

hands.name: Order inflow growth, year on year
hands.meaning: Slowing inflow with a full book is late-cycle; a rising inflow with a rising book is mid-cycle

clock.so_what: Mid-boom is when margins expand but valuations already assume it, so the money is made in names whose order book is still growing faster than their sales.

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track government capex and power demand; together they decide how long the grid and generation ordering wave lasts.

bottlenecks.name: Electrical steel import dependence
bottlenecks.why: Transformer cores need cold-rolled grain-oriented steel, which India barely makes. Supply comes from Japan, Korea and China and is rationed in a global shortage.

bottlenecks.name: Transformer capacity shortage
bottlenecks.why: Large transformers take years to build and nobody added capacity through the bust. Good for incumbents' prices, bad for project timelines.

bottlenecks.name: Fixed-price contracts
bottlenecks.why: Project builders quote a price today for work that runs for years; a metal or wage spike lands on their margin, not the customer's.

bottlenecks.name: Payment delays from state utilities
bottlenecks.why: State power distribution companies pay late, so receivables balloon and the contractor finances the government.

bottlenecks.name: Land, forest and right of way
bottlenecks.why: Transmission lines and plants stall for years waiting for land and forest clearances, which delays billing on orders already won.

bottlenecks.name: Chinese price competition
bottlenecks.why: Chinese makers undercut on boilers, turbines, solar equipment and now transformers; India keeps them out with duties and procurement rules, not cost.

bottlenecks.name: Election and budget calendar
bottlenecks.why: Government ordering stops for two quarters around a general election and slows in the first quarter of every fiscal year.

bottlenecks.name: Skilled engineers and welders
bottlenecks.why: Every site competes for the same supervisors and certified welders when the whole country is building at once.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two bottlenecks are why the grid door is earning record margins; the next three are why the project door is not.

rulebook.body: Ministry of Power and Central Electricity Authority
rulebook.what: National transmission plan, thermal and hydro capacity targets, grid connectivity
rulebook.why: Decides the size of the biggest order pipeline in the sector

rulebook.what: Approve utility tariffs and capex recovery
rulebook.why: A utility can only order what the regulator lets it recover from consumers

rulebook.body: Public procurement preference and the restricted-country rule
rulebook.what: Make-in-India preference in government tenders and curbs on bidders from countries sharing a land border
rulebook.why: Keeps Chinese equipment out of grid and PSU tenders, protecting domestic prices

rulebook.what: Mandatory standards on imported cables, motors, transformers and components
rulebook.why: A tariff by another name for the electricals door

rulebook.body: Production-linked incentives and the electronics and solar schemes
rulebook.what: Cash incentives for domestic manufacturing in chosen sectors
rulebook.why: Creates factory capex, which is orders for machine and automation makers

rulebook.body: Approved list of models and manufacturers for solar
rulebook.what: Only listed domestic makers can supply government-backed solar projects
rulebook.why: Shifts renewable equipment orders to Indian plants

rulebook.body: Railway Board and the railway budget
rulebook.what: Annual electrification, rolling stock and signalling programmes
rulebook.why: A steady order source that swings with the budget, not the market

rulebook.body: Energy-efficiency rules for motors and transformers
rulebook.what: Minimum efficiency standards that retire old equipment
rulebook.why: Forces replacement demand even without new capacity

rulebook.what: Duties on Indian steel products, forgings and components
rulebook.why: Hits the export share of the component door

why.rivalry: Three or four makers of large transformers with full books; dozens of contractors bidding lowest price on every tender
why.supplier: Electrical steel comes from a few foreign mills and is rationed; metals are pass-through for builders
why.buyer: Utilities need equipment now and accept price rises; the same utilities dictate terms to contractors in a tender
why.entrants: Qualification, type testing and reference lists take years; new EPC firms appear every cycle
why.substitutes: Nothing replaces a transformer; a buyer can split a project or self-execute instead of hiring a builder

forces.so_what: The equipment makers keep most of the profit in this cycle because the shortage is theirs; the project builders keep little and give some back when a contract goes wrong.

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the book is still filling
cheat_sheet.good: Above 15% y/y; a decline for two quarters is the first late-cycle sign

cheat_sheet.tells: Years of visible work
cheat_sheet.good: 2–3× for equipment, 3–4× for project builders; falling means sales are eating the book

cheat_sheet.tells: Pricing power and execution together
cheat_sheet.good: Equipment 15%+ and rising; builders 9–12% and stable

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether metal prices are being passed on
cheat_sheet.good: Stable q/q within 2 points when copper moves

cheat_sheet.tells: Who is paying late
cheat_sheet.good: Under 90 days for equipment; builders under 150 and not rising

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the book is converting to revenue
cheat_sheet.good: Above 15% while inflows also grow; execution not just booking

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the growth earns its capital
cheat_sheet.good: Equipment above 25%; builders above 15%

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether capacity is being added into the shortage
cheat_sheet.good: Above 1.5× for transformer makers now; near 1× is coasting on the shortage

lead_indicators.name: Union budget capital outlay

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when order inflows outgrow sales, equipment delivery times are long, and private capex is joining public capex; all three means boom, two means mid-cycle, one means the book is running down.

call.headline: Mid-cycle boom with earnings catching up to prices. Prefer grid equipment and electricals names with growing books over project builders, and be choosy on valuation.
points: Grid and generation ordering is the strongest it has been in fifteen years and the transformer shortage gives equipment makers pricing power.
Margins are expanding as old low-price orders roll off, which is the sweet spot of the cycle for equipment names.
Project builders carry the same demand but keep less of it, and a single stuck contract can erase a year of margin.
would_change: Two straight quarters of falling order inflows at the large names
Transformer lead times shortening as new global capacity arrives
A sharp cut in government capex or a long election-style ordering pause

explainer.tell_a_friend: Capital goods companies make the machines that make everything else: transformers for the grid, boilers and turbines for power plants, motors and automation for factories, cables for buildings. Their business comes in waves because it depends on who is building. From 2012 to 2019 nobody was, and the sector was dead money. Since 2021 the government has spent heavily on railways, roads and especially the power grid, because India keeps running short of electricity and has to connect huge solar and wind farms. On top of that the whole world is short of transformers, so the companies that make them can name their price. Profits are now rising fast and the stocks have already priced in a lot. The simplest split is this: companies that sell equipment off a waiting list keep fat margins, companies that build whole projects for a fixed price keep thin ones and sometimes lose money on a bad contract. Watch order inflows against sales, delivery times for transformers, and whether private factories start spending too.

glossary.def: Machines and equipment bought to produce something else, not to consume: a turbine, a transformer, a lathe.
New orders won in the quarter. The sector's leading indicator.
Orders won but not yet executed. Divided by yearly sales it gives years of visible work.
Order inflow divided by sales in the same period. Above 1 means the book is growing.
Engineering, procurement and construction: one contractor designs, buys and builds the whole project for a price.
A contract where the price is set at signing. Input cost rises come out of the contractor's margin.
Transmission and distribution: the wires, towers, transformers and substations that carry electricity from plant to plug.
Equipment that changes voltage so power can travel long distances and then enter homes. Big ones take 2–3 years to build.
The switches and breakers that control and protect an electrical circuit, from a household board to a substation.
Cold-rolled grain-oriented steel, the special sheet inside transformer cores. India imports nearly all of it.
Everything in a power plant other than the boiler, turbine and generator.
Money tied up in unpaid customer bills, retention money and work done but not yet billed, minus supplier bills and customer advances.
A slice of each bill, often 5–10%, that the customer holds back until the project is proven to work.
Money a buyer pays upfront when placing an order. It funds the maker's working capital and earns interest meanwhile.
Sales minus materials, as a share of sales. Shows whether metal price moves are being passed on.
Operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation, as a share of sales.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by equity plus debt. Equipment makers run 25%+ because they own few assets.
Yearly spending on new plant divided by the depreciation charge. Above 1 means capacity is growing.
Production-linked incentive: a government cash payout tied to incremental factory output in chosen industries.
The approved list of models and manufacturers: only solar equipment on it can be used in government-backed projects.
A procurement rule requiring prior approval for bidders from countries sharing a land border with India, in practice China.
The legal permission to run a transmission line or pipeline across land. The slowest step in any grid project.
A diesel or gas generator set used as backup or primary power by factories, telecom towers and buildings.

explainer.one_liner: Logistics companies move India's stuff: they run the ports where ships unload, the trains and trucks that carry containers and coal inland, the warehouses where goods wait, and the vans that drop a parcel at your door.

doors.name: Ports, airports and terminals
doors.sub: Own or lease the gateway under a long concession and charge a fee per tonne, container, passenger or litre stored; volume growth with near-fixed costs
doors.blurb: A bet on India's trade and travel volumes passing through a gate you own for decades

doors.name: Rail freight and rail builders
doors.sub: Haul containers on Indian Railways' tracks, or build and consult on railway lines for the state; the customer and the landlord are both the government
doors.blurb: A bet on the railway budget, the freight corridors and the shift of cargo from road to rail

doors.name: Express and e-commerce parcels
doors.sub: Pick up, sort and deliver millions of small parcels for e-commerce and businesses, paid per shipment; a volume and density game with thin margins
doors.blurb: A bet on online shopping growth winning out over the price war among carriers

doors.name: Shipping
doors.sub: Own tankers, bulk carriers and offshore vessels and rent them out at a daily rate the world market sets
doors.blurb: A bet on global freight rates and ship prices, with India as an afterthought

explainer.door_analogy: Door one owns the only bridge into town and takes a toll from every cart. Door two runs carts on the government's road and sometimes builds the road. Door three is the delivery boy paid a few rupees per packet, competing with every other delivery boy. Door four owns the carts and rents them out at whatever the market pays that week.
explainer.door_so_what: A port stock is a toll collector, a parcel stock is a price war, a shipping stock is a commodity, so the word logistics on its own tells you nothing about what you are buying.

stations.name: Origin
stations.what: A factory, mine, farm or overseas supplier has goods ready to move; an e-commerce seller has an order
stations.who: Exporters, importers, coal and cement producers, Amazon, Flipkart and Meesho sellers

stations.name: Gateway
stations.what: Cargo enters or leaves the country through a port or airport, or fuel and chemicals are stored at a terminal
stations.who: ADANIPORTS, JSW and the state-owned major ports, GPPL, GMRAIRPORT, AEGISLOG, AEGISVOPAK; Singapore, Colombo and Dubai as the transhipment rivals

stations.name: Line haul
stations.what: Goods move long distance by rail, truck or ship between hubs
stations.who: Indian Railways and CONCOR by rail, millions of small truck owners by road, GESHIP and SCI at sea; foreign shipping lines carry most of India's containers

stations.name: Hub and warehouse
stations.what: Cargo is sorted, stored, bundled and dispatched from inland container depots, sorting centres and warehouses
stations.who: CONCOR depots, DELHIVERY and SHADOWFAX sorting hubs, third-party warehouse operators

stations.name: Last mile
stations.what: The parcel or the truckload reaches the shop, factory or doorstep
stations.who: DELHIVERY, SHADOWFAX, BLUEDART, the post office and a huge unorganised fleet of small transporters

kitchen.rival: Foreign shipping lines and the Colombo, Singapore and Dubai transhipment hubs
kitchen.note: Gujarat handles the biggest slice of India's cargo, with Mundra the largest port, and the western freight corridor now ties it to the Delhi industrial belt by rail. Container shipping to and from India is mostly in foreign hands, which is why a new Indian transhipment port at Vizhinjam matters.
kitchen.so_what: The gateways and the last mile are where Indian listed names stand and where the profit pools are; the long-haul leg between them is dominated by the state railway and foreign lines, so Indian investors mostly cannot buy it.

explainer.end_markets_so_what: A port name reads the trade data and the coal numbers, a parcel name reads e-commerce order counts, so look at the customer before the quarter.

lines.why: Tonnes, containers, parcels and the rate on each; the whole sector is volume times price per unit
Ports, airports, ships and wagons are heavy assets built upfront; depreciation and interest eat most of what the toll collectors earn
Concession assets are debt-funded for decades; a shipping name's fate turns on how much debt it carried into the downturn
A port or airport earns little per rupee of asset but for very long; a parcel network earns a lot per rupee of asset but keeps little
Light for ports where customers pay upfront; heavy for rail builders waiting on government bills
Bunker fuel for ships, diesel for trucks and haulage charges for rail are the cost lines that swing with crude
Indian Railways sets what a container operator pays to use the track, and a hike can erase a year of margin
Government rail companies earn interest on client advances, and it can be a quarter of their profit

pnl.analogy: A port is a toll plaza: it cost a fortune to build, costs little to run, and every extra truck is nearly pure profit. A parcel company is a tiffin service: each delivery earns a few rupees, and the game is to make the same van carry more tiffins per street.
pnl.so_what: For toll collectors read volume growth and EBITDA margin; for parcel names read shipments and cost per shipment; for shipping read the day rate and the debt.

clock.is_cyclical: Partly. Shipping is violently cyclical with world freight rates, ports and parcels are steady growers that wobble with trade and consumption, and rail builders follow the railway budget rather than any market cycle.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Covid breaks supply chains, containers run short, freight rates multiply several times and shipping companies print record profits; e-commerce volumes jump as everyone shops from home

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Freight rates top out, logistics start-ups list at rich valuations and everyone orders new ships and builds warehouses

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Freight rates collapse to pre-Covid levels, e-commerce growth slows, parcel carriers fight a price war and the listed start-ups fall by more than half

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Volumes keep growing while prices stay weak; Red Sea diversions put a floor under shipping rates and port cargo hits records

clock.position_detail: volumes at records, parcel prices still weak

timeline.what: The GST and e-way bill have cleaned up interstate trucking and larger warehouses replace one-per-state godowns. Trade is soft and the shadow-bank crisis hits truck financing.
Lockdowns empty the ports for a quarter, then e-commerce explodes and containers run short worldwide. Shipping rates begin a historic climb.

The boom. Container rates multiply, Indian shipping names earn in a year what they used to earn in five, Delhivery lists, and the National Logistics Policy promises to cut India's logistics cost as a share of GDP.
The bust. Freight rates fall back to earth, e-commerce slows, parcel carriers undercut each other and the first stretches of the dedicated freight corridors open to traffic.
Red Sea attacks force ships around Africa and rates rebound. Port cargo hits records. Railway PSU stocks go on a speculative run on budget hopes and then give much of it back.

Vizhinjam opens as India's first deep-water transhipment port, the western freight corridor is nearly complete, quick commerce changes how parcels move in cities and shipbuilding gets its own policy push.

Ports and terminals compound steadily, new listings bring liquid terminals and a gig-delivery network to the market, and rail builders export rakes again. The parcel price war has eased but not ended.

clock.so_what: Early up-cycle here is volume-led: the toll collectors benefit first, the parcel names only once pricing recovers, and shipping only if world rates hold.

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track port cargo growth and crude oil; one tells you the volume, the other the cost.

bottlenecks.name: Rail haulage and track access
bottlenecks.why: Indian Railways owns the track, sets the haulage charge and runs its own freight; private container operators are tenants who can be squeezed overnight.

bottlenecks.name: Road share too high
bottlenecks.why: Most Indian cargo still goes by truck, which is slower and costlier than rail; moving it to the freight corridors is the whole national logistics plan and it takes a decade.

bottlenecks.name: Fragmented trucking
bottlenecks.why: Millions of owner-drivers with one or two trucks set a brutal price floor; no organised player can hold a premium for long.

bottlenecks.name: Transhipment leaks abroad
bottlenecks.why: A large share of India's containers change ships at Colombo, Singapore or Dubai because Indian ports lacked depth; Vizhinjam is the first real answer.

bottlenecks.name: Concession and regulatory risk
bottlenecks.why: Ports and airports live under decades-long government agreements; a tariff ruling, a revenue-share dispute or a land fight can reset the economics.

bottlenecks.name: Parcel price wars
bottlenecks.why: E-commerce platforms squeeze carriers, in-house logistics arms take volume and gig networks undercut; yields fall every time a new entrant is funded.

bottlenecks.name: Monsoon and festive seasonality
bottlenecks.why: Cargo and parcels bunch into the second half of the year; a weak first half is often the calendar, not the business.

bottlenecks.name: Government bills paid late
bottlenecks.why: Rail builders and consultants wait on PSU and ministry payments, which bloats receivables and makes profit a function of cash, not work.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two are why ports and corridors are the long-term story; the sixth is why parcel names keep disappointing.

rulebook.body: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and the Major Port Authorities
rulebook.what: Governs the state-owned major ports, port tariffs and the Sagarmala port programme
rulebook.why: Sets the competing price at major ports and awards new terminals

rulebook.body: Concession agreements with state maritime boards
rulebook.what: Decades-long rights to build and run a private port, with a revenue share to the state
rulebook.why: The moat and the risk of every private port name live in one document

rulebook.body: Ministry of Railways and the freight-corridor company
rulebook.what: Owns the track, sets haulage charges, runs the dedicated freight corridors
rulebook.why: Landlord to the container operators and customer to the rail builders

rulebook.body: National Logistics Policy and PM GatiShakti
rulebook.what: Plan to cut logistics cost, build multimodal parks and coordinate infrastructure
rulebook.why: Decides where warehouses, parks and corridors get built

rulebook.what: Fixes aeronautical charges at the big airports for five-year blocks
rulebook.why: A tariff order can swing an airport operator's earnings for years

rulebook.what: One national tax and an electronic permit for goods in transit
rulebook.why: Killed the state-border checkposts and let warehouses consolidate; organised players gained

rulebook.what: Reviews mergers and abuse of dominance
rulebook.why: Watches the largest port operator's acquisitions and e-commerce platforms' logistics arms

rulebook.body: Shipbuilding assistance and the maritime development fund
rulebook.what: Subsidies and finance for building ships in India, plus a coastal shipping law
rulebook.why: Props up Indian-flag shipping and orders for domestic yards

rulebook.what: Rules on which ships may carry coastal cargo and a right of first refusal for Indian ships
rulebook.why: Protects Indian shipowners' home market from foreign lines

why.rivalry: A port competes with the next port a few hundred kilometres away; a parcel carrier competes with everyone, including its customers' own fleets
why.supplier: Ports buy little; parcel carriers depend on gig workers, fuel and leased trucks whose prices they do not set
why.buyer: Shipping lines negotiate but need the gateway; e-commerce platforms dictate rates to carriers
why.entrants: A new port needs a coastline, a concession and a decade; a new parcel network needs funding and a year
why.substitutes: Cargo can shift port or mode slowly; a platform can insource delivery overnight

forces.so_what: The gateway owners keep the profit because nobody can build a second coastline; the parcel carriers hand theirs to the platforms and the customer.

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the network is getting busier
cheat_sheet.good: Ports 8–12% y/y; parcels 15%+

cheat_sheet.tells: Pricing power per tonne, container or parcel

cheat_sheet.tells: The operating leverage of the asset
cheat_sheet.good: Ports 60–70%; container rail 20%+; express 5–10% and rising

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the asset's debt is comfortable

cheat_sheet.tells: How much of operating profit the lenders take
cheat_sheet.good: Under 25%

cheat_sheet.tells: Building new capacity or sweating the old
cheat_sheet.good: Above 1.5× when utilisation is above 70%; below 1× otherwise

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the government or platforms are paying
cheat_sheet.good: Ports under 30; rail builders under 120 and not rising

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the heavy asset earns its keep
cheat_sheet.good: Ports 15%+; express positive and improving; rail builders 15%+

lead_indicators.channel: Published before results; tonnage is revenue the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: Export and import data
lead_indicators.channel: Containers move with trade the same month

lead_indicators.name: Coal and power demand
lead_indicators.channel: Coal stocks at plants decide bulk cargo next quarter

lead_indicators.name: E-commerce gross order value and festive sale commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Platform orders are next quarter's parcels

lead_indicators.name: Global container and tanker rate indices
lead_indicators.channel: Charters are signed ahead; today's rate is next quarter's shipping revenue

lead_indicators.name: Railway budget and freight-corridor commissioning
lead_indicators.channel: Budget lines become rail builders' orders and container-train volumes

lead_indicators.name: Crude oil price
lead_indicators.channel: Fuel costs pass to the P&L with a one-quarter lag on contracts

lead_indicators.name: Warehouse leasing data from property consultants

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when port cargo is growing, parcel yields are stable or rising, and freight rates are holding; three of three is a boom, two is a volume-led recovery, one is a false dawn.

call.headline: Volume-led early up-cycle. Prefer the toll collectors, ports and terminals, over parcel carriers and shipping until parcel pricing and freight rates both turn.
points: Port and terminal volumes are at records and their costs are mostly fixed, so growth drops straight to profit.
Parcel carriers have the volume but not the price; the war has eased, not ended, and platforms keep insourcing.
Rail builders depend on a railway budget that is high but no longer growing fast, so order inflow is the number to watch, not the stock's PSU label.
would_change: A global trade slowdown or tariff shock cutting container volumes
A fresh funded entrant in parcels reopening the price war
A rail haulage hike or concession dispute hitting a listed operator

explainer.tell_a_friend: Logistics companies move India's stuff, and the trick is to notice they are four very different businesses. Ports, airports and storage terminals are toll gates: they cost a fortune to build, almost nothing extra to run, and every extra container or passenger is nearly pure profit. Rail freight and rail builders live off Indian Railways, which is both their landlord and their customer. Parcel companies deliver your online orders for a few rupees each and fight a permanent price war with each other and with the platforms' own fleets. Shipping companies own vessels and earn whatever the world rate is that week. Covid created a boom in 2021 and 2022, then rates and e-commerce cooled in 2023 and the start-ups fell hard. Now port volumes are at records, the freight corridors are nearly complete and parcel pricing has stopped falling. Buy the toll gates for the long run, read port cargo and crude oil every month, and treat shipping as a trade, not an investment.

glossary.def: A long government contract, often 30 years, to build and run a port, airport or road, sharing some revenue with the state.
Moving a container from one ship to another at a hub port. India's boxes often do this at Colombo or Singapore.
Twenty-foot equivalent unit, the standard container measure. A 40-foot box is 2 TEU.
New rail lines built only for goods trains, so freight no longer waits behind passenger trains.
The fee Indian Railways charges a container operator to run a train on its track. Set by the Railways alone.
A dry port inland where containers are stuffed, cleared by customs and loaded onto trains.
Moving one shipment by more than one mode, say ship then rail then truck, under one contract.
Courier, express and parcels: time-bound delivery of small shipments, mostly e-commerce.
The final leg from the local hub to the doorstep. The most expensive part of a parcel's journey.
Revenue earned per parcel. Falling yield means a price war.
A company that runs warehousing and transport for a manufacturer or retailer under contract.
The daily hire rate for a ship. Set by the world market and highly volatile.
The heavy fuel oil ships burn. The biggest cost for a ship owner after the ship itself.
The rule that coastal cargo between two Indian ports should move on Indian-flag ships.
Tanks at a port that store LPG, fuels and chemicals for a fee per tonne or per month.
The electronic permit that must travel with any goods consignment under GST. Replaced state border checkposts.
Operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation, as a share of revenue. Ports run 60–70%.
Borrowings divided by yearly operating profit. Years needed to repay debt from operations.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by equity plus debt.
Grocery and goods delivered within minutes from dark stores in the city, bypassing the national parcel network.
The government's port-led development programme: new ports, coastal shipping and port connectivity.
One of the dozen large state-owned ports under the central government, as against private or state-government ports.

explainer.one_liner: Airlines rent planes, fill them with passengers and fuel, and try to land with a little money left over; in India one carrier does this well, the rest struggle, and a handful of charter, helicopter and drone operators fly around the edges.

doors.name: Scale low-cost airline
doors.sub: One aircraft type, high seat density, planes in the air most of the day, fares sold online with every extra charged; wins on cost per seat
doors.blurb: A bet on India's travel growth landing in the hands of the carrier with the lowest cost and the most slots

doors.name: Sub-scale airline
doors.sub: A small, ageing or grounded fleet, late payments to lessors and staff, survival funded by promoters, courts and new investors
doors.blurb: A bet on a rescue, not on the industry

doors.name: Charter, helicopter and air services
doors.sub: Fly business jets, helicopters for oil rigs and pilgrims, and private charters on contract or per hour
doors.blurb: A bet on corporate travel, offshore oil work and government contracts, with a small fleet and lumpy earnings

doors.name: Drones and aerial data
doors.sub: Fly unmanned aircraft to survey farms, mines and pipelines and sell the data or the service
doors.blurb: A bet on a rulebook that keeps loosening and on a few paying customers turning into many

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the state bus corporation that runs the same bus on every route, packed, from dawn to midnight. Door two is a bus operator whose vehicles are half in the workshop and whose drivers are owed salary. Door three is the taxi hired by the hour. Door four is a drone photographer still convincing clients to pay.
explainer.door_so_what: In Indian aviation the industry's growth and one company's profit are almost the same thing, so you are buying a near-monopoly on a thin margin, not a sector.

stations.name: Aircraft and engines
stations.what: Planes are ordered years ahead, financed by lessors and powered by engines the airline does not make
stations.who: Airbus and Boeing, with Pratt and Whitney and CFM engines; Irish, Chinese and Indian lessors; GIFT City leasing just beginning

stations.name: Fuel
stations.what: Aviation turbine fuel is bought from the oil companies at prices that move with crude and with state taxes
stations.who: Indian Oil, BPCL, HPCL; crude price set abroad

stations.name: Airports and air traffic
stations.what: Slots, landing, parking and passenger fees at airports; airspace managed by the state
stations.who: Airports Authority of India, GMR and Adani airports; Pakistan and the Gulf when airspace closes

stations.name: The airline
stations.what: Crew, scheduling, selling tickets, turning the plane in under an hour
stations.who: INDIGO, SPICEJET, FLYSBS, GLOBALVECT; Air India and Akasa unlisted; Gulf carriers on international routes

stations.name: Maintenance and the passenger
stations.what: Heavy checks and engine shop visits, mostly abroad; passengers book through online agents and the airline's app
stations.who: Foreign MRO shops in Singapore, the Gulf and Europe; Indian MRO growing; MakeMyTrip and the airline's own site

kitchen.rival: Gulf carriers on international routes; Air India as the unlisted domestic rival
kitchen.note: Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru carry a large share of all passengers and slots there are the scarcest asset in the industry. Almost everything an airline buys is priced in dollars, from the plane to the engine overhaul, while almost every ticket is sold in rupees.
kitchen.so_what: The airline stands at the fourth station but controls none of the first three, so its margin is whatever is left after Airbus, the oil companies and the airports have been paid.

end_markets.name: Leisure travellers
end_markets.buys: Domestic holiday and festival flights, booked weeks ahead on price
end_markets.moves_with: Middle-class income, fares, festival and wedding calendars

end_markets.name: Business travellers
end_markets.buys: Last-minute trunk-route tickets at higher fares
end_markets.moves_with: Corporate activity, IT and financial services hiring, video calls

end_markets.name: Visiting friends and relatives
end_markets.buys: Tier-two city connections and international Gulf and Southeast Asia flights
end_markets.moves_with: Migration, remittances, Gulf employment

end_markets.name: International and connecting passengers
end_markets.buys: Long-haul and hub flights, now including Indian carriers' own widebodies
end_markets.moves_with: Visa regimes, bilateral seat rights, Gulf carrier capacity

end_markets.name: Cargo shippers
end_markets.buys: Belly space and freighters for pharma, electronics, perishables
end_markets.moves_with: Exports, e-commerce, sea-freight disruption

end_markets.name: Government and oil companies
end_markets.buys: Helicopter and charter contracts for rigs, pilgrim routes, VIP movement
end_markets.moves_with: Offshore drilling, state budgets, elections

end_markets.name: Farmers, miners and utilities
end_markets.buys: Drone surveys and spraying
end_markets.moves_with: Drone rules, subsidy schemes, input prices

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Domestic leisure is the volume and business travel is the margin, so a quarter with full planes and low fares is a leisure quarter, not a profitable one.

lines.why: Fares times load factor; the industry's one top-line number

lines.line: Cost per available seat kilometre excluding fuel
lines.why: The airline's own cost discipline, stripped of the oil price; the number that separates the two airline doors
Around a third of cost, moves with crude, the dollar and state taxes, and cannot be hedged well in India
Planes are leased, so rent shows up as depreciation and interest under accounting rules; it is the second-largest cost
Lease liabilities are in dollars, so a weaker rupee creates a loss even when nothing operational changed
Passengers pay before they fly, so a growing airline holds customer cash; a shrinking one bleeds it
Low because the fleet is rented; a new airline can start with a credit card and a lessor
Engine makers pay airlines for grounded planes, and that income can be a big slice of a reported profit

pnl.analogy: An airline is a wedding caterer who has already rented the hall and paid the cooks before a single guest confirms. Every extra plate sold is nearly pure profit, every empty chair is pure loss, and the price of gas is decided by somebody else.
pnl.so_what: Read the gap between revenue per seat kilometre and cost per seat kilometre, then check how much of the reported profit came from grounding compensation rather than flying.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, and brutally. Demand grows steadily but profit swings with crude, the rupee and how many seats the competitors added; the industry has made money in only a handful of years and lost it in most.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Crude collapses, fares hold, passenger growth runs high teens and the largest carrier lists and earns its best margins

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Every airline orders hundreds of planes, capacity floods in, crude climbs back and the rupee slides; margins vanish

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: The second-largest carrier collapses, then Covid grounds the entire fleet; the industry loses more in two years than it had earned in a decade

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Fare caps, half-empty planes and the national carrier sold to a private group; only the strongest balance sheet is still ordering aircraft

clock.position_detail: fares high, grounded planes returning

timeline.what: Jet Airways stops flying and fares jump. The market consolidates around one low-cost carrier before anyone planned it.
Covid grounds the fleet, the regulator caps fares and capacity, and Air India is finally sold to the Tatas. The bottom of the cycle.
Travel roars back, a new low-cost carrier launches, fare caps are lifted and crude spikes after the Ukraine invasion; volumes recover faster than profits.

A low-cost rival goes bankrupt blaming its engine supplier, dozens of planes across the industry are grounded for engine inspections, fares rise and the leader posts its first big annual profit while placing the largest aircraft order in history.
Record passenger numbers and record profit for the leader. Air India merges its airlines and starts a fleet overhaul. Groundings keep supply tight and fares firm.

A Dreamliner crash at Ahmedabad shakes confidence and triggers safety audits. Pakistan closes its airspace after the May conflict, lengthening westbound flights. The leader begins long-haul flying with leased widebodies.

The leader is financing new Airbus deliveries, adding long-range single-aisle jets for Europe and growing international share. The sub-scale carrier is in court over dues and its pilots refuse to fly over unpaid salaries. Grounded planes are returning, so the capacity squeeze is easing.

hands.name: Domestic passengers, year on year
hands.meaning: Faster growth with capacity flat means fares rise; growth below capacity adds means fares fall

hands.name: Grounded aircraft count
hands.meaning: Fewer groundings add seats and soften fares, but cut compensation income

hands.name: Crude oil in rupees
hands.meaning: A sustained rise eats margin within a quarter; a fall is the industry's best news

hands.name: Air India and new-entrant capacity additions
hands.meaning: Rival seats added faster than demand grows is how every past boom ended

clock.so_what: A capacity-constrained boom rewards the carrier that already has the planes and the slots, and ends when the rivals' planes finally arrive.

dials.name: Crude oil
dials.channel: Aviation fuel, about a third of cost
dials.rise_does: cuts margin within a quarter

dials.name: Dollar against the rupee
dials.channel: Leases, maintenance, fuel and the mark-to-market on lease liabilities
dials.rise_does: raises costs and books foreign-exchange losses

dials.name: Middle-class income and consumer confidence
dials.channel: Leisure and family travel demand
dials.rise_does: fills planes at better fares

dials.name: Interest rates abroad
dials.channel: Aircraft lease rates and financing
dials.rise_does: makes new planes dearer to rent

dials.name: Business activity
dials.channel: Corporate travel, the high-fare passenger
dials.rise_does: lifts yields on trunk routes

dials.name: Geopolitics and airspace closures
dials.channel: Longer routes, more fuel, cancelled flights
dials.rise_does: adds cost to international flying

dials.name: Engine and aircraft delivery delays
dials.channel: How many seats the industry can add
dials.rise_does: keeps fares high but caps growth

dials.name: State taxes on aviation fuel
dials.channel: Fuel cost varies by state of uplift
dials.rise_does: raises the fuel bill at that airport

dials.name: Airport charges and capacity
dials.channel: User fees and slots at the big three airports
dials.rise_does: adds cost but new terminals add growth

dials.name: Transport inflation
dials.channel: What passengers see fares doing
dials.rise_does: signals pricing power, risks a policy response

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track crude oil and the dollar-rupee rate; together they are half of an airline's cost base and they move the same way at the worst times.

bottlenecks.name: Engine groundings
bottlenecks.why: A large share of the new-generation fleet has been grounded in rotation for engine inspections and parts shortages, with planes waiting months for a spare engine.

bottlenecks.name: Slots at the big airports
bottlenecks.why: Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are full at peak hours; a new entrant cannot buy its way in, and the incumbent's slot bank is its real moat.

bottlenecks.name: Dollar costs, rupee revenue
bottlenecks.why: Planes, engines, spare parts and overhauls are priced in dollars while tickets are sold in rupees, so the currency decides a year's result.

bottlenecks.name: Aviation fuel taxes
bottlenecks.why: Fuel is taxed by each state and sits outside GST, so Indian airlines pay among the highest fuel prices anywhere.

bottlenecks.name: Maintenance goes abroad
bottlenecks.why: Heavy checks and engine shop visits happen in Singapore, the Gulf or Europe because India lacks the shops and the tax treatment, adding cost and downtime.

bottlenecks.name: Pilots and crew
bottlenecks.why: Training a captain takes years, poaching is rife and duty-time rules tightened by the regulator shrink the effective roster.

bottlenecks.name: Safety incidents and audits
bottlenecks.why: One crash or a run of incidents brings regulator audits, fleet inspections and a demand dip that hits the whole industry, not just the airline involved.

bottlenecks.name: Fare caps and political pressure
bottlenecks.why: The government has capped fares before and summons airlines whenever festival fares spike; pricing power is tolerated, not guaranteed.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The slot moat and the engine shortage are why one airline earns money today; the dollar and the fuel tax are why even that airline keeps so little of it.

rulebook.what: Safety oversight, airworthiness, pilot duty-time rules, airline licences
rulebook.why: Can ground a fleet, cap flying hours or audit an airline after an incident

rulebook.what: Policy, bilateral seat rights, fare monitoring, the regional connectivity scheme
rulebook.why: Decides who flies abroad and whether fares get capped

rulebook.what: Fixes landing, parking and passenger fees at major airports
rulebook.why: A tariff order moves airline costs and airport profits for five years

rulebook.body: Airports Authority of India and private airport operators
rulebook.what: Own and run airports, allocate slots
rulebook.why: Slot allocation is the scarcest input in the industry

rulebook.what: Subsidised routes to small towns with fare caps and airport fee waivers
rulebook.why: Creates demand for regional planes and helicopter routes; margins depend on the subsidy

rulebook.what: Lets lessors repossess aircraft quickly when an airline defaults
rulebook.why: Lowers lease costs for everyone and removes a weapon weak airlines used to delay

rulebook.what: Tax-advantaged leasing from an Indian offshore zone
rulebook.why: Begins to move a dollar cost line onshore

rulebook.body: Drone rules and the drone PLI
rulebook.what: Light-touch registration, airspace maps and a subsidy for drone makers
rulebook.why: Opened the drone door and keeps widening it

rulebook.what: State VAT on fuel, outside GST
rulebook.why: A move into GST would be the single biggest margin event for airlines

why.rivalry: Two serious players and a fringe; the leader sets fares, the sub-scale carrier must match them with higher costs
why.supplier: Two plane makers, two engine makers and a few lessors; they are paid first and in dollars
why.buyer: Passengers compare every fare online and have no loyalty; the leader at least owns the slots they need
why.entrants: Anyone with funding can lease planes, but slots at the big airports and a decade of cost learning cannot be bought
why.substitutes: Trains and video calls on short routes; the new fast trains are a real threat on the busiest city pairs

forces.so_what: Suppliers keep most of the profit in aviation; the one airline with scale keeps a thin slice, and the rest keep nothing.

cheat_sheet.good: Above 85% domestic; above 90% is pricing power

cheat_sheet.tells: Fares and fullness together
cheat_sheet.good: Rising y/y; a fall with high load factor means fares are being cut

cheat_sheet.metric: Cost per seat kilometre, ex fuel
cheat_sheet.tells: The airline's own discipline
cheat_sheet.good: Flat or falling in rupees; rising faster than inflation is a warning

cheat_sheet.metric: Fuel as a share of sales
cheat_sheet.tells: Exposure to crude and the rupee
cheat_sheet.good: Under 35% of revenue

cheat_sheet.tells: Operating profit after fuel and before planes
cheat_sheet.good: Above 20% including lease rentals at the leader; positive at all for others

cheat_sheet.tells: What is left after leases, interest and currency
cheat_sheet.good: 5–10% in a good year; the industry average over a decade is near zero

cheat_sheet.metric: Employee cost as a share of sales
cheat_sheet.tells: Crew productivity and wage pressure
cheat_sheet.good: Under 10% of revenue

cheat_sheet.tells: How much profit came from not flying
cheat_sheet.good: Groundings falling, compensation under 10% of profit

lead_indicators.name: Crude oil and the rupee
lead_indicators.channel: Fuel is bought at spot and lease liabilities revalue each quarter

lead_indicators.name: Monthly domestic passenger data from the regulator
lead_indicators.channel: Published mid-month; traffic is revenue the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: Fleet grounding count and engine-maker delivery guidance
lead_indicators.channel: Decides how many seats the industry has next quarter and how firm fares stay

lead_indicators.name: Air India and new-entrant delivery schedules
lead_indicators.channel: Rival seats arriving in two quarters set the fare war odds

lead_indicators.name: Hotel occupancy and travel-portal booking commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Forward bookings show leisure demand before it flies

lead_indicators.name: Corporate hiring and IT services commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Business travel is the high-fare passenger

lead_indicators.name: Lessor and global airline capacity commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Lease rates and plane availability shape the cost of growth

lead_indicators.name: Geopolitical flare-ups near air corridors
lead_indicators.channel: Airspace closures add hours and fuel the same week

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when passenger growth outruns seat additions, crude in rupees is flat or falling, and the balance sheet is adding planes without adding debt; three of three means the rare profitable year, two means fragile, one means a fare war is coming.

signs.name: Crude in rupees flat or falling

call.headline: A capacity-constrained boom that is one airline's story. Own the leader if you own the sector at all, size it for the fare war that follows every Indian aviation boom, and treat the rest as rescue trades.
points: Demand is growing high single digits with fares firm because grounded planes have kept supply tight.
The leader's cost per seat, slot bank and order book are structural; its profit is still hostage to crude and the rupee.
Air India's fleet overhaul and returning grounded planes are the next capacity wave, and capacity waves end Indian aviation booms.
would_change: Crude falling sharply with a stable rupee, which would extend the boom
Rival capacity landing faster than passenger growth, which would start the fare war early
A safety-driven grounding or airspace shock at the leader

explainer.tell_a_friend: Airlines are a bad business that India loves: planes, engines, parts and overhauls are all paid in dollars, fuel is a third of cost and taxed by every state, and passengers buy whichever ticket is cheapest online. The industry has made money in a handful of years and lost it in most. What makes India different is that one low-cost carrier has become so large and so cheap to run that it owns the best slots and most of the market, while its rivals went bankrupt in 2019 and 2023. Since 2023 a global engine problem has kept dozens of planes grounded, so seats are scarce, fares are high and the leader has posted record profits. Covid in 2020 was the bottom, this is the boom. The question is what happens when the grounded planes come back and the newly private Air India gets its new fleet: every past Indian aviation boom has ended in a fare war. Watch crude in rupees, monthly passenger growth against seat additions, and how much of the profit is compensation for planes that are not flying.

glossary.def: An airline with one aircraft type, dense seating, fast turnarounds and extras sold separately, so cost per seat stays low.
An airline with business class, free meals and lounges, charging higher fares to cover higher costs. In India, mainly Air India.
Seats sold divided by seats flown. 85% means 85 of every 100 seats had a passenger.
Available seat kilometres: seats flown times distance. The industry's measure of capacity.
Revenue per available seat kilometre: total revenue divided by capacity. Fares and fullness in one number.
Cost per available seat kilometre. Often quoted ex fuel to show the airline's own efficiency.
Average fare per passenger kilometre. Rises when planes are full and competitors are short of seats.
Aviation turbine fuel, the kerosene jets burn. Priced monthly by the oil companies and taxed by each state outside GST.
A company that owns aircraft and rents them to airlines, usually for 6–12 years in dollars.
An airline buys a plane at a bulk discount, sells it to a lessor at a gain and rents it back. A source of profit for big-order airlines.
The future rent on leased planes, booked as debt. Revalued every quarter as the rupee moves, creating foreign-exchange gains or losses.
Taking an aircraft out of service, here because its engine needs inspection or a spare is not available.
Money an engine maker pays an airline for planes it cannot fly. Shows up as other income.
A permitted take-off or landing time at an airport. At Delhi and Mumbai, scarce and effectively owned by incumbents.
Government-to-government agreements on how many seats each country's airlines may fly between them. Caps Gulf carriers' growth.
Maintenance, repair and overhaul: heavy checks and engine shop visits, mostly done abroad for Indian fleets.
Twin-aisle long-haul jets versus single-aisle jets. Indian carriers are mostly narrowbody; widebodies are the new international push.
The regional connectivity scheme: subsidised, fare-capped routes to small-town airports.
A global treaty letting lessors repossess aircraft fast on default. India legislated it in 2025 to lower lease costs.
Aircraft leasing from India's offshore financial zone in Gujarat with tax breaks, so some leases move onshore.
Directorate General of Civil Aviation, the safety regulator that licenses airlines, pilots and aircraft.
Airport Economic Regulatory Authority, which fixes the fees big airports may charge airlines and passengers.

explainer.one_liner: Defence companies build fighter jets, warships, missiles, radars and the electronics inside them for one customer, the Indian armed forces, and are now being pushed to make at home what India used to import and to sell some of it abroad.

doors.name: State-owned platform primes
doors.sub: Design, integrate and deliver whole aircraft, missiles and electronic systems on multi-year government contracts, paid in milestones with large advances upfront
doors.blurb: A bet on the defence budget, on the government preferring its own factories, and on delivery not slipping

doors.name: Shipyards
doors.sub: Build destroyers, frigates, submarines and patrol vessels over five to ten years each, on fixed-price contracts with big customer advances
doors.blurb: A bet on the navy's fleet plan and on finishing ships early enough to keep the incentive

doors.name: Private electronics and sub-systems
doors.sub: Design and make radar modules, missile electronics, optics and test systems as a supplier to the primes and the research labs
doors.blurb: A bet on the primes outsourcing more, with small order books that double or halve on one contract

doors.name: Aerospace parts and structures
doors.sub: Precision-machine engine parts, tooling, airframe pieces and hangars for Indian and global aircraft makers
doors.blurb: A bet on global aerospace supply chains adding India, more than on the Indian military

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the government's own kitchen that cooks every state banquet. Door two builds the banquet hall itself, one every few years. Door three supplies the spice mixes and the ovens to the kitchen. Door four makes cutlery for restaurants in India and abroad.
explainer.door_so_what: The primes have the orders and the cash, the shipyards have the longest visibility and the slowest conversion, and the private names have the growth and the lumpiness, so the same budget headline moves each door differently.

stations.name: Research and design
stations.what: The government's labs and the primes' design bureaus draw the aircraft, missile or radar; foreign partners supply what India cannot yet design, above all engines
stations.who: DRDO labs, HAL and BEL design centres; GE, Safran and Rolls-Royce for engines; Russia, France and Israel for licensed designs

stations.name: Materials and components
stations.what: Special steels, titanium, composites, chips, optics and seekers come in, much of it imported
stations.who: Midhani for alloys, PARAS for optics, APOLLO and DATAPATTNS for electronics; Israel, the US and Europe for sensors and chips

stations.name: Sub-system making
stations.what: Components become radar modules, missile guidance, sonar, hull blocks, machined engine parts
stations.who: DATAPATTNS, APOLLO, UNIMECH, KRISHNADEF, hundreds of small private vendors around Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune

stations.name: Platform integration
stations.what: Sub-systems are assembled into a fighter, a frigate, a missile battery, a radar network and tested
stations.who: HAL, BEL, BDL, MAZDOCK, COCHINSHIP, GRSE, SWANDEF; the government's quality agencies at every step

stations.name: Delivery, upkeep and export
stations.what: The forces take delivery; the maker supports it for decades and sells spare versions abroad
stations.who: Army, navy and air force; HAL and BEL service depots; export customers in Southeast Asia, Africa and the Gulf

kitchen.rival: Foreign original equipment makers, above all US, French, Russian and Israeli, who still supply engines, sensors and the big-ticket imports
kitchen.note: Bengaluru is the aerospace capital, Hyderabad the missile and electronics hub, and the shipyards sit in Mumbai, Kochi, Kolkata, Visakhapatnam and Goa. The foreign content hides in the engines and sensors, so a fighter stamped Made in India may still depend on a delivery from Ohio.
kitchen.so_what: India has largely nationalised the last two stations; the profit and the delay both come from the first two, where the engine and the sensor still arrive from abroad.

end_markets.name: Indian Air Force
end_markets.buys: Fighters, trainers, helicopters, transport aircraft, radars, missiles
end_markets.moves_with: Squadron shortfalls, the capital budget, engine deliveries from abroad

end_markets.name: Indian Navy
end_markets.buys: Destroyers, frigates, submarines, carriers, patrol craft, sonar and combat systems
end_markets.moves_with: The fleet plan, Chinese naval activity in the Indian Ocean, shipyard capacity

end_markets.name: Indian Army
end_markets.buys: Artillery, tanks and vehicles, anti-tank and air-defence missiles, radios, drones, night vision
end_markets.moves_with: Border tension with China and Pakistan, emergency procurement powers

end_markets.name: Paramilitary, coast guard and police
end_markets.buys: Patrol vessels, small arms, surveillance, communications
end_markets.moves_with: Home ministry budgets, coastal security pushes

end_markets.name: Export customers
end_markets.buys: Missiles, radars, patrol vessels, light helicopters, artillery
end_markets.moves_with: Government-to-government deals, lines of credit, rivals' delivery backlogs

end_markets.name: Space and ISRO
end_markets.buys: Launch vehicle structures, satellite electronics, ground systems
end_markets.moves_with: Launch cadence, the opening of space to private firms

end_markets.name: Global aerospace majors
end_markets.buys: Machined parts, tooling, sub-assemblies for civil and military aircraft
end_markets.moves_with: Airbus and Boeing production rates, supply-chain diversification away from China

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Three services and one ministry make almost every buying decision, so the industry's demand is a policy choice, not a market, and it can be accelerated or frozen by a single committee meeting.

lines.why: The book is the next five to ten years of revenue; a big contract signing is the single most important event in a stock's year
Orders only matter if they turn into delivered aircraft and ships; execution, not demand, is the constraint
Imported kits carry no margin; the more a prime designs and sources at home, the more it keeps
The forces pay a large share upfront; the interest on that cash can be a fifth of a shipyard's profit and flatters margins
Negative for shipyards because of advances; heavy for private suppliers who wait on the primes and the labs to pay
Factories are old and largely depreciated at the PSUs; small for the private names
New production lines for fighters and new dry docks are the capex that unlocks the book; otherwise asset-light
Almost all listed names are debt-free and sit on cash; interest is income, not cost
Late deliveries attract penalties and lost incentives; the shipyards' margin swings on finishing early or late

pnl.analogy: A defence prime is a caterer with one wealthy client who pays half the bill before the wedding, so the caterer earns interest on the client's money while cooking slowly. The risk is not the client leaving; it is the oven, imported, arriving late.
pnl.so_what: Read order book against sales for visibility, revenue growth for execution, and then strip the interest on advances out of the profit to see what the factories actually earn.

clock.is_cyclical: Not a market cycle; a policy cycle. Demand is set by the defence budget, the share of it spent at home and the pace of approvals, with border conflicts as the accelerator and procurement scandals as the brake.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Post-Kargil modernisation money flows, big import deals are signed and the PSU primes grow fat on licensed production

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: The helicopter bribery scandal, blacklisted vendors and a cautious ministry; orders pile up in committees

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Procurement freezes, the fighter tender collapses into a small off-the-shelf buy and the primes list to a cold market; HAL's shares fall below issue

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: A cash crunch at the aircraft prime, then the Galwan clash and the first import-ban lists reset the whole policy toward buying Indian

clock.position_detail: record order books, deliveries lag engines

timeline.what: Balakot air strikes and a fleet of ageing fighters expose the squadron gap. The aircraft prime borrows to pay salaries while waiting on government dues. The stocks are unloved.
The Galwan clash with China changes everything. Emergency buying powers are used, the first list of weapons that may no longer be imported is published and foreign ownership limits are raised.
The big home-built fighter order is signed, a new procurement manual favours Indian design, defence corridors are set up and exports are pushed with a hard target. Order books begin to swell.
Exports hit records, the navy commissions its first home-built carrier, private suppliers list and re-rate, and the sector becomes the market's favourite theme.

Order placement slows into the election and valuations hit extremes; the stocks correct sharply from the peak even as order books stay full. Engine deliveries from the US slip, delaying fighter output.

Operation Sindoor in May proves home-made missiles and air defence in combat and drives emergency orders. A further fighter batch, carrier-borne jets from France and the submarine programme are cleared. The stocks rally back.

Order books at the primes stand at several years of sales, brokers list the primes among their top picks into the results season, and the shipyards hold record advances. The constraint is engines and delivery, not demand.

hands.name: Defence capital budget growth
hands.meaning: Faster growth means more approvals become contracts this year

hands.name: Order book to sales at the primes
hands.meaning: Rising visibility is good only if execution keeps pace

hands.name: Engine and import deliveries
hands.meaning: Late engines mean fighters built but not delivered, which means revenue slips a year

hands.name: Export order wins
hands.meaning: Exports prove competitiveness and loosen the one-customer problem

clock.so_what: An execution-paced boom means revenue, not orders, is the surprise variable, and a stock can fall on a record order book if deliveries slip.
