kitchen.so_what: Because most retail is still unorganised, the listed chains can grow for years simply by taking share, but quick-commerce apps are a new rival for urban grocery and impulse buys.

pnl.analogy: A retailer is a vegetable vendor with a cart: the profit on each tomato is small, but if the cart empties three times a day the vendor does well. If tomatoes rot on the cart, the day is lost.
pnl.so_what: Read same-store sales growth and inventory days together: rising same-store sales with lean stock is the healthy pattern, while growth from new stores alone hides a tired format.

clock.is_cyclical: Mildly. Groceries barely cycle; fashion and jewellery swing with household confidence, food inflation and gold prices. The bigger force is structural: organised retail taking share from unorganised shops.

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when same-store sales are accelerating, food inflation is easing, and store expansion is holding returns; two of three means recovery, one of three means a stall.

call.headline: Early up-cycle helped by tax relief. Prefer value fashion and organised jewellery chains taking share from local shops; be selective in urban grocery, where quick commerce is squeezing.
points: Tax cuts and lower GST have put money back in household wallets just as festive season arrives.
Organised players still hold a small share, so store expansion in small towns has a long runway.
Quick commerce is a structural rival for big-box grocery in the metros.

explainer.tell_a_friend: Retailers rent or buy shops, fill them with groceries, clothes, shoes or gold, and sell at a markup. The money comes from turning stock over quickly and keeping each store busy. India is huge but organised chains still hold only a small slice; most shopping happens at kiranas and local shops, so the chains can grow for years just by opening more stores, especially in small towns. Fashion chains with their own brands earn the most per rupee of sales. Grocery chains earn little per item but sell a lot. Jewellers live on weddings, trust and the gold price. After a weak 2023 and 2024, when food inflation ate into wallets, tax cuts in 2025 brought shoppers back. The new worry is quick-commerce apps delivering groceries in minutes. Watch same-store sales, food inflation and the gold price.

glossary.def: Sales growth from stores open for at least a year; strips out the effect of new stores.
Chains and branded stores that pay GST and report numbers, as opposed to kiranas and local shops.
A family-run neighbourhood grocery store.

The number of people walking into a store.

Sales minus the cost of the goods sold, divided by sales.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: operating profit before paying for stores or loans.
Stock divided by sales, times 365: how long goods sit before selling.
The fee a jeweller adds on top of the gold value for crafting the piece; the jeweller's real margin.
A BIS stamp certifying gold purity; mandatory since 2021.
Borrowing gold from a bank instead of cash to hold as inventory, which hedges price swings.
A diamond made in a factory; chemically the same as mined but far cheaper.
Low-priced own-brand clothing for mass buyers, like Zudio or Vishal.
Selling through stores, website and app with shared stock and returns.
Time a new store takes to earn back its setup cost; under 3 years is good.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested.
Rule that puts store rent on the balance sheet, so rent appears as depreciation and interest.

explainer.one_liner: E-commerce companies put a shop, a restaurant, a job board or a railway counter inside your phone, take a small cut of every order, and spend enormous sums on riders, warehouses and discounts so that you keep coming back.

doors.name: Delivery marketplaces
doors.sub: A cut of every food or grocery order, plus ads from restaurants and brands, minus the rider and the dark store
doors.blurb: A bet that order frequency rises faster than the cost of the last mile

doors.name: Classifieds and listings
doors.sub: Recruiters, sellers and dealers pay a subscription or a listing fee; the platform owns no stock and delivers nothing
doors.blurb: A bet on a network that is already the default, so every extra rupee is nearly all profit

doors.name: Own-stock vertical retailers
doors.sub: Buy or make the product, sell it online and in stores, keep the full retail margin and carry the inventory
doors.blurb: A bet on a brand and a category, where the website is just the shopfront

doors.name: Toll booths
doors.sub: A tiny fee per ticket, per order or per truck trip on a very large number of transactions
doors.blurb: A bet on volume and on nobody changing the toll

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is a dabbawala who also runs the kitchen's advertising. Door two is the newspaper's classifieds page, now on a phone. Door three is a shop that happens to have a very long queue outside its website. Door four is the toll plaza on the highway: small change, every car, every day.
explainer.door_so_what: A delivery name is valued on how fast its losses shrink, a classifieds name on how high its margin already is, a vertical retailer on store economics, and a toll booth on whether anyone can touch the toll, so the same results headline means different things behind each door.

lines.line: Gross order value and take rate
lines.why: Revenue is a cut of what flows through; growth in flow times the cut is the whole top line, and ad income lifts the cut without hurting the seller
What is left after the rider, the packaging and the discount; the first number that turns positive in a delivery business and the one the stock trades on
The dial management turns to buy growth; a quarter of soaring orders with soaring marketing is bought, not earned
Marketplaces collect from the customer today and pay the seller later, so cash arrives before cost; own-stock retailers carry months of inventory instead
Dark stores, warehouses and store fit-outs now sit on the balance sheet; the shift to owning inventory makes this line grow
Dark-store roll-outs are the capex line; a store takes two to three quarters to mature, so a build phase depresses margins while the future improves
A large, non-cash charge that keeps reported profit far below adjusted profit; read both numbers
Almost every listed name is net cash from its IPO; interest is other income, not a cost

pnl.analogy: A delivery platform is a wedding caterer who is paid a fixed cut per plate but pays each waiter per plate carried; the business works only when the hall is full. A classifieds site is the hall owner: once built, every extra booking is nearly pure profit.
pnl.so_what: Read contribution margin per order and marketing spend together: margin up with marketing flat is real operating leverage, margin up with marketing down is harvesting, and margin flat with marketing up is a price war.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, but to the funding cycle rather than the economic one. When global money is cheap, platforms raise, burn and grow; when rates rise, the money stops, the discounts stop and the weakest players fold or sell.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Lockdowns push grocery, food and beauty online; cheap global money funds a listing wave led by Zomato and Nykaa

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Loss-making platforms list at record valuations and every category gets a ten-minute delivery start-up

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Rate hikes end cheap money, platform stocks fall by well over half, the funding winter starts and Zomato buys a distressed Blinkit

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Platforms pivot to profit, food delivery turns positive, discounts fade and the survivors consolidate

clock.position_detail: profits arriving, valuations full, quick-commerce war easing

timeline.what: A tighter FDI press note bars foreign-owned marketplaces from owning stock or favouring sellers, and Amazon and Flipkart restructure around it. Food delivery is a two-horse race funded by discounts.
COVID-19 moves groceries, medicines and dinner onto the phone for good. Cheap global money arrives, Zomato lists in 2021 to a frenzy and Nykaa follows; quick commerce is born as a ten-minute promise.

The bust. Global rates rise, the funding winter sets in, Zomato's stock falls to a fraction of its listing price and it buys Blinkit cheaply. Every platform swaps growth slides for profitability slides.
The bottom. Food delivery turns profitable, Blinkit becomes the surprise growth engine, and the stocks begin a long climb.
A second listing wave starts: Ixigo, FirstCry, Swiggy and Blackbuck list. Quick commerce becomes the hottest category in Indian consumer and dark-store counts double.

Zomato renames itself Eternal and moves Blinkit to owning its own stock after the FDI cap is eased. The quick-commerce war with Zepto and Instamart peaks in losses. Urban Company, Lenskart, Meesho and Wakefit list; a new GST charge lands on delivery services.

Eternal is the year's standout large-cap on narrowing quick-commerce losses and strong food-delivery profit, Nykaa and Meesho hold their IPO gains, and FSSAI is moving to make online food players directly accountable. Valuations are full and the sector trades on execution, not hope.

bottlenecks.name: Last-mile cost
bottlenecks.why: A human on a bike carries every order, so the cost per delivery falls only with density. Below a certain number of orders per rider per hour, growth adds losses.

bottlenecks.name: Amazon and Flipkart's balance sheets
bottlenecks.why: The two largest rivals are unlisted in India and funded by foreign parents who can lose money for a decade. Price discipline is borrowed, not owned.

bottlenecks.name: Funding-driven competition
bottlenecks.why: Every time global money is cheap a new entrant arrives with discounts; Zepto did it in quick commerce and Rapido is doing it in food delivery.

bottlenecks.name: Policy on foreign ownership
bottlenecks.why: The marketplace versus inventory rule is rewritten every few years, and each rewrite reshuffles who may own stock and who may not.

bottlenecks.name: Gig-worker regulation
bottlenecks.why: State gig-worker welfare laws, the labour codes and GST on delivery fees each add a few rupees per order, which is the whole contribution margin.

bottlenecks.name: Dark-store real estate
bottlenecks.why: The right two thousand square feet near rich flats is scarce and rents rise with every competitor's expansion.

bottlenecks.name: Kirana and dealer pushback
bottlenecks.why: Trader associations lobby against deep discounting and quick commerce, and the government listens before elections.

bottlenecks.name: Stock-option dilution
bottlenecks.why: Large annual option grants quietly transfer a slice of the company from shareholders to employees every year.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The first two never go away and cap margins for delivery names; the funding cycle decides when the next price war starts, so watch rivals' fund-raises as closely as results.

why.rivalry: Two or three delivery platforms fight for the same flat with the same riders and discounts; a classifieds leader is usually alone in its category
why.supplier: Riders can switch apps mid-shift and restaurants can delist; recruiters and sellers have nowhere else with the same audience
why.buyer: Customers keep two delivery apps and switch for a coupon; a recruiter cannot leave the biggest resume pool
why.entrants: A funded entrant can buy share in delivery within a year; building a classifieds network from scratch has failed repeatedly
why.substitutes: The kirana, the restaurant's own app and ONDC are substitutes for delivery; LinkedIn and job portals of the big IT firms nibble at classifieds

forces.so_what: Classifieds keeps most of the profit because its network is the moat, delivery keeps the least because the rider and the rival set the price, which is why a classifieds name earns high margins at a lower multiple while a delivery leader earns thin margins at a very high one.

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when contribution margins are expanding, marketing as a share of revenue is falling, and global yields are steady or lower; two of three means the rally rests on fundamentals, one of three means it rests on liquidity.

call.headline: Boom phase with real profits underneath. Prefer the leaders with proven unit economics and the asset-light classifieds names; treat freshly listed loss-makers as execution bets priced for perfection.
points: Food delivery is profitable and quick-commerce losses are narrowing at the leader, so the stock story has moved from hope to delivery.
The listing wave of 2024 and 2025 added a dozen names at full valuations; the market will sort them on contribution margin, not on gross order value.
Regulation is tightening at the edges: GST on delivery, gig-worker levies and FSSAI accountability each shave the margin per order.
would_change: A sharp rise in global yields that re-rates growth stocks and reopens the funding winter
A new, well-funded entrant restarting the quick-commerce discount war
A rewrite of the FDI or digital-competition rules that removes the Indian-owned platforms' edge

explainer.tell_a_friend: E-commerce companies put a shop, a restaurant or a railway counter inside your phone and take a cut of every order. The trick is that someone on a bike still has to carry the parcel, so a delivery platform makes money only when a neighbourhood is dense enough that one rider carries several orders an hour. A job board or a seller directory has no rider at all, which is why it earns fat margins. The sector runs on the global funding cycle rather than the Indian economy: when money was cheap in 2020 and 2021, platforms listed at wild prices and burned cash on discounts. When rates rose in 2022 the stocks collapsed and the survivors learned to make a profit. Food delivery turned profitable in 2023, quick commerce became the new battlefield, and a second wave of listings arrived in 2024 and 2025. Today profits are real but prices are full. Watch contribution margin per order, marketing as a share of revenue, and the US ten-year yield.

glossary.def: The total rupee value of everything bought through the platform. The platform's revenue is a slice of this, not the whole.
The platform's revenue as a share of gross order value: commissions plus ads plus fees, divided by GOV.
Revenue per order minus the direct cost of that order (rider, packaging, discount, payment fee). The first profit line to turn positive.
Operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and the stock-option charge. The number platforms prefer to headline.
A small warehouse closed to walk-in customers, stocked for ten-to-thirty-minute delivery to flats within a two-to-three kilometre radius.
Grocery and essentials delivered within minutes from a dark store: Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto.
The platform connects buyers and sellers and never owns the goods. Foreign-owned platforms in India were long restricted to this.
The platform buys and owns the stock it sells, keeping the full retail margin and the inventory risk.
Government rules on how much a foreign-owned online platform may own and whether it may hold stock; rewritten in 2018-19 and eased in 2025.
A listings business: recruiters, sellers or dealers pay to be found. The platform sells visibility, not goods.
A small fixed charge per ticket booked online. For IRCTC and Ixigo it is most of the profit.
A rider or service professional paid per task through an app, without an employment contract.

glossary.term: Social Security Code and gig-worker laws
glossary.def: Central and state laws requiring platforms to contribute 1-2% of each transaction to a welfare fund for gig workers.
App designs that trick users into paying more or subscribing: fake urgency, hidden fees, basket sneaking. Banned by the consumer-protection regulator in 2023.
Central Consumer Protection Authority, the enforcement arm under the Department of Consumer Affairs.
Competition Commission of India, the antitrust regulator probing preferential treatment and deep discounting by big platforms.
Open Network for Digital Commerce, a government-backed network meant to let any seller reach any buyer app without a single marketplace in between.
Shares granted to staff that vest over years. Charged as an expense, which is why reported profit trails adjusted profit.
The period from 2022 when venture capital dried up after global rate rises, forcing start-ups to cut burn.
The number of distinct customers who placed at least one order in a month.
The final leg from dark store or hub to the customer's door, carried by a rider. The most expensive kilometre.
Cash and investments minus borrowings. For listed platforms, the war chest left from the IPO.

explainer.one_liner: Consumer durables companies make or brand the things a household buys once every few years and finances on EMI: the air-conditioner, the fridge, the fan, the television, the wedding gold and the branded innerwear.

doors.name: Appliance brand owners
doors.sub: Design and market the AC, fridge, fan or water heater; often buy the box from a contract maker; sell through dealers who keep a fat cut
doors.blurb: A bet on the summer, the brand's shelf share and the copper price

doors.name: Contract manufacturers
doors.sub: Assemble phones, TVs, ACs and washing machines for brands under the PLI scheme at a thin, fixed margin on very high volumes
doors.blurb: A bet on volume, asset turns and the China+1 shift in electronics, not on margins

doors.name: Lifestyle brand owners
doors.sub: Own the brand and the shop: jewellery, premium innerwear, home textiles and stationery sold at a price the brand sets
doors.blurb: A bet on aspiration and on the brand's pricing power through a slowdown

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the restaurant whose name is on the board and whose menu sets the price. Door two is the central kitchen that cooks for a dozen restaurants at a fixed rate per plate. Door three is the jeweller down the lane whose customers come back for the name on the box.
explainer.door_so_what: Ask which door a stock is behind before you read its margin, because a brand owner's single-digit operating margin is normal, a contract maker's low-single-digit margin is the model, and a lifestyle brand's high-teens margin is the moat.

stations.name: Raw materials and components
stations.what: Copper, aluminium, steel, plastic resin, compressors, display panels, printed circuit boards and chips come in, mostly by ship
stations.who: Chinese compressor and panel makers, metal importers, Hindalco and the steel mills

stations.name: Assembly
stations.what: Components become a finished AC, TV, phone, washing machine or fan on an assembly line
stations.who: DIXON, AMBER, PGEL, and the brands' own plants

stations.name: Brand and design
stations.what: The product gets a name, a warranty, a star rating and an ad campaign
stations.who: LGEINDIA, VOLTAS, BLUESTARCO, WHIRLPOOL, CROMPTON, VGUARD, TITAN, PAGEIND

stations.name: Distribution and retail
stations.what: Distributors, dealers, large-format chains, online marketplaces and brand stores take their cut
stations.who: Croma, Reliance Digital, Vijay Sales, Amazon, Flipkart, Tanishq stores

stations.name: Household and financier
stations.what: The family buys on a festival weekend, often on a zero-cost EMI
stations.who: Urban and Tier-2 households, Bajaj Finance and the banks

kitchen.rival: China
kitchen.note: Assembly clusters sit near Noida and Greater Noida for electronics, Sri City and Chennai for ACs and phones, and Pune and Ahmedabad for white goods; jewellery is made in Hosur and Coimbatore. The compressor, the panel and the chip are still largely imported, so the cost line starts at the port.
kitchen.so_what: India assembles but does not yet make the heart of the machine, so a weaker rupee or a Chinese export curb on compressors lands on Indian margins within a quarter.

end_markets.name: Households cooling down
end_markets.buys: Air-conditioners, coolers, fans, refrigerators
end_markets.moves_with: How hot and how early the summer is, power supply, EMI availability

end_markets.name: New homes being fitted out
end_markets.buys: Fans, lighting, water heaters, kitchen appliances, wires
end_markets.moves_with: Housing completions, repainting and renovation cycles

end_markets.name: Weddings and festivals
end_markets.buys: Gold and diamond jewellery, watches, gifts
end_markets.moves_with: Gold price, wedding dates on the calendar, farm incomes

end_markets.name: Global phone and electronics brands
end_markets.buys: Assembled smartphones, TVs, laptops and set-top boxes made under contract
end_markets.moves_with: Smartphone demand, PLI incentives, brands shifting production out of China

end_markets.name: Aspirational wardrobes
end_markets.buys: Premium innerwear, athleisure, branded home textiles
end_markets.moves_with: Urban discretionary income, online fashion growth, cotton prices

end_markets.name: Western retailers
end_markets.buys: Towels and bedsheets made in India for Walmart, Target and Costco
end_markets.moves_with: US housing and retail inventory, US tariffs, cotton prices

end_markets.name: Shops, offices and cold chains
end_markets.buys: Commercial refrigeration, ductable ACs, chillers
end_markets.moves_with: Retail and pharma capex, data centres, government buildings

end_markets.name: Schools and offices
end_markets.buys: Pencils, pens, art and stationery supplies
end_markets.moves_with: The school calendar and exports to Europe

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Most of this demand is weather, calendar or credit, not income, so a late monsoon, a thin wedding season or a tighter EMI market tells you the quarter before the results do.

lines.why: Copper, aluminium, steel and imported components are two thirds of a brand owner's sales; a commodity spike shows up here within a quarter and price hikes follow with a lag
Brand owners spend a few per cent of sales to hold shelf share; a cut flatters margins this year and costs share next year
Dealers are stuffed before summer and cleared after it, so inventory and receivable days swing with the season; a washed-out summer leaves channel stock that kills the next two quarters
Contract makers live on turning assets many times a year; a new PLI plant depresses turns for a year before it fills
Low for brand owners who outsource; rising for contract makers and for anyone building backward into compressors and components
Brand owners are mostly net cash; contract makers and jewellers borrow to fund inventory, and Titan's gold-on-lease cost sits here
Net-cash brand owners earn treasury income that can be a fifth of profit in a bad year
Nothing sector-specific; the GST line is on the customer's bill, not the P&L

pnl.analogy: A brand owner is a mithai shop before Diwali: it buys sugar and ghee at whatever the market charges, prints boxes months ahead and prays the festival is busy. A contract maker is the halwai cooking in the back for five shops at a fixed rate per kilo; he gets rich only by cooking a lot.
pnl.so_what: Read channel inventory and gross margin together after every summer and every Diwali: a clean channel with stable gross margin means the next season starts fresh, a stuffed channel means two quarters of discounts first.

clock.is_cyclical: Yes, on two clocks at once. A seasonal one, where the summer and the festive quarter decide the year, and a slower one tied to commodity prices, interest rates and policy pushes such as PLI and GST cuts.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Work-from-home buys TVs and laptops, a record 2022 summer sells out ACs, and PLI makes Dixon the China+1 poster child

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Every brand announces capacity, channel inventory is built for a repeat summer, and commodity costs peak at the same time

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Unseasonal rain washes out the summer, dealers sit on stock, discounts return and margins compress

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Channel clears, input costs ease, and the heatwave summer of 2024 restarts the cycle with record cooling volumes

clock.position_detail: channel clean, tax cut, summer decides

timeline.what: Slow demand, tighter energy labels and a weak festive season. The compressor, the panel and the phone are still mostly imported.

COVID-19 kills the AC summer in its first quarter, then work-from-home drives TVs, laptops and kitchen appliances. The government bans imports of filled ACs and announces PLI for components and phones.

The boom. A second wave hurts the 2021 summer but the 2022 summer is a record, Dixon and Amber scale under PLI, and stocks re-rate as the China+1 electronics story takes hold. Copper and steel prices squeeze margins all the while.
The bust. Rain in March, April and May washes out the cooling season, dealers are left with stock, and brand owners discount for two quarters.
A heatwave summer sells a record number of ACs, Dixon doubles on the smartphone PLI ramp, and Titan rides a gold-price surge. The channel is cleared and capacity is announced again.

An early monsoon washes out the summer again and AC volumes fall by a quarter or more. Then the GST Council cuts the rate on ACs, large TVs and dishwashers from the top slab to the standard slab before Diwali, and LG Electronics India lists in a large IPO.

The tax cut and a clean channel reset demand, premium cooling and compressor localisation are the capex themes, Titan keeps growing on a record gold price while Page Industries waits for volumes. The sector is early in a new up-leg that the summer will confirm or deny.

hands.name: Channel inventory after the season
hands.meaning: Clean means the next season starts fresh; stuffed means two quarters of discounts

hands.name: Copper and aluminium prices
hands.meaning: Rising means gross margin squeeze until price hikes catch up

hands.name: Volume growth after the GST cut
hands.meaning: Sustained means the tax cut created demand, not just a pull-forward

hands.name: Contract makers' asset turns
hands.meaning: Rising means new plants are filling; falling means capacity ran ahead of orders

clock.so_what: Early up-cycle after two bad summers rewards the brand owners first, because their margins have the most room to recover, while contract makers need the new plants to fill before the stocks move again.

dials.name: Copper price
dials.channel: The biggest single input in ACs, fans, motors and wiring
dials.rise_does: squeezes brand owners' gross margin for a quarter or two

dials.name: Summer heat and its timing
dials.channel: Air-conditioner, cooler and fan volumes
dials.rise_does: sells out the cooling season

dials.name: Interest rates
dials.channel: EMI cost and the share of purchases on credit
dials.rise_does: slows big-ticket purchases and festive volumes

dials.name: Rupee against the dollar
dials.channel: Imported compressors, panels and chips
dials.rise_does: weaker rupee raises component cost

dials.name: Gold price
dials.channel: Jewellery demand and inventory gains
dials.rise_does: lifts ticket size, trims grammage, helps Titan's inventory

dials.name: Housing completions
dials.channel: Fans, lights, water heaters and kitchen appliances for new homes
dials.rise_does: lifts the fitting-out categories a few quarters later

dials.name: Aluminium and steel
dials.channel: Fridge and washing-machine bodies, heat exchangers
dials.rise_does: adds to the input squeeze

dials.name: Industrial output of durables
dials.channel: Coincident read on factory volumes
dials.rise_does: confirms the volume quarter

dials.name: US tariffs and US retail
dials.channel: Home-textile and electronics exports
dials.rise_does: hurts Welspun's US business

dials.name: Crude oil
dials.channel: Plastic resin, packaging and freight
dials.rise_does: adds a small input squeeze

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track the copper price and the summer; copper sets the margin and the summer sets the volume, and together they explain most years.

bottlenecks.name: Imported heart of the machine
bottlenecks.why: Compressors, display panels and chips are still mostly imported from China and East Asia. India assembles the box but does not yet make the part that costs the most.

bottlenecks.name: Weather risk
bottlenecks.why: A single rainy April can wipe out a third of the year's AC profit, and there is no hedge for it.

bottlenecks.name: Dealer and channel power
bottlenecks.why: Distributors and large-format chains take a fat margin and return unsold stock; online marketplaces squeeze further on price.

bottlenecks.name: Thin contract margins
bottlenecks.why: A contract maker earns a few rupees per unit on a product the brand prices; one lost brand account or one PLI target missed changes the year.

bottlenecks.name: Low penetration, slow conversion
bottlenecks.why: Only a small minority of Indian homes own an AC, which is the long-term opportunity, but power supply, flat sizes and incomes make the conversion slower than the pitch suggests.

bottlenecks.name: Commodity pass-through lag
bottlenecks.why: Prices are set for the season and raw-material contracts for the quarter, so cost spikes hit margins before price hikes arrive.

bottlenecks.name: Policy whiplash
bottlenecks.why: Import bans, quality-control orders, star-label revisions and GST rate changes each reset the market within months.

bottlenecks.name: Gold price and hallmarking
bottlenecks.why: A sharp gold rally cuts the grams sold even as it inflates sales, and hallmarking rules reshape the unorganised competition.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: The imported core and the dealer's cut set the margin ceiling; the weather and policy whiplash are the quarterly surprises worth a news alert per company.

rulebook.what: Sets the tax slab on each appliance; cut ACs, large TVs and dishwashers from the top slab to the standard slab in 2025
rulebook.why: A ten-point tax cut is the biggest demand event in a decade; a reversal would be the biggest risk

rulebook.what: Mandatory Indian standards on ACs, fans, TVs, toys and components, including imports
rulebook.why: Works like a tariff on cheap imports and favours local assembly

rulebook.what: Energy-efficiency ratings that tighten every couple of years, plus default-temperature rules for ACs
rulebook.why: Each tightening raises cost per unit and favours inverter makers

rulebook.body: PLI schemes under MeitY and DPIIT
rulebook.what: Cash incentives on incremental output of phones, IT hardware, AC and LED components
rulebook.why: The reason Dixon, Amber and PG Electroplast exist at their current size; the component scheme is the next leg

rulebook.what: Import ban on filled ACs, duties and quotas on components
rulebook.why: Shapes what must be made in India and what may be imported

rulebook.body: Kigali phase-down via the environment ministry
rulebook.what: Quotas on HFC refrigerant gases with an Indian freeze from 2028
rulebook.why: Forces a shift to new gases and compressors, with cost and redesign

rulebook.what: Extended producer responsibility: brands must collect and recycle a share of what they sell
rulebook.why: A cost line that grows every year

rulebook.body: BIS hallmarking and gold import duty
rulebook.what: Mandatory hallmarking with a unique ID on gold jewellery; the duty on imported gold
rulebook.why: Hallmarking pushes buyers to organised jewellers; a duty cut moves demand within a quarter

rulebook.what: Right-to-repair portal, warranty and e-commerce rules
rulebook.why: Raises after-sales obligations for brands

why.rivalry: A dozen Indian, Korean, Japanese and Chinese brands fight for the same dealer shelf; a few large contract makers compete on price per unit but each brand prefers two suppliers
why.supplier: Compressors, panels and chips come from a handful of Chinese and East Asian makers who set the price
why.buyer: Dealers and online marketplaces squeeze brands on margin and returns; a contract maker's customer is a global brand that dictates price and can walk
why.entrants: Reliance, Chinese brands and start-ups keep entering appliances; PLI invites a new contract maker every year
why.substitutes: There is no substitute for a fridge, but a longer replacement cycle is the hidden substitute in a slowdown

forces.so_what: Lifestyle brands keep the most because the customer pays for the name, appliance brand owners keep a modest slice after the dealer and the commodity, and contract makers keep the least and must make it up on volume, which is why the market pays contract makers for growth and brand owners for margins.

cheat_sheet.tells: The commodity squeeze versus pricing power
cheat_sheet.good: Brand owners 28-35% and stable; contract makers 8-12%

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether the season or the tax cut delivered
cheat_sheet.good: Double-digit unit growth in cooling and in PLI categories

cheat_sheet.metric: Advertising as a share of sales
cheat_sheet.tells: Whether margins are being bought by cutting the brand
cheat_sheet.good: Steady at 2-4% of sales for brand owners

cheat_sheet.tells: Channel health after the season
cheat_sheet.good: Falling after the summer; below 60 days for brand owners

cheat_sheet.tells: Dealer stuffing
cheat_sheet.good: Stable; a jump after a weak season means the channel was pushed

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether contract makers' plants are filling
cheat_sheet.good: Above 5× for contract makers, rising on new plants

cheat_sheet.tells: Whether a thin margin still earns its keep
cheat_sheet.good: Above 20% for brand and lifestyle names; above 25% for contract makers on high turns

cheat_sheet.tells: Build or coast
cheat_sheet.good: Above 2× when backward-integrating into compressors or components, with turns holding

lead_indicators.name: Weather forecasts for March to May
lead_indicators.channel: An early, hot forecast means dealers stock up and the June quarter sells through

lead_indicators.name: Copper and aluminium futures
lead_indicators.channel: Raw-material contracts reset a quarter after the metal moves

lead_indicators.name: Housing completions and repainting commentary
lead_indicators.channel: New homes buy fans, lights and kitchen appliances two quarters after possession

lead_indicators.name: Smartphone brand shipment guidance
lead_indicators.channel: Samsung, Xiaomi and Motorola volumes are Dixon's order book

lead_indicators.name: Bajaj Finance consumer-durable loan growth
lead_indicators.channel: EMI financing moves with purchases the same quarter

lead_indicators.name: Gold price and the wedding calendar
lead_indicators.channel: Jewellery grammage reacts to price the same month; wedding dates set the quarter

lead_indicators.name: US retailers' inventory commentary
lead_indicators.channel: Walmart and Target destocking is Welspun's next quarter

lead_indicators.name: GST Council and BIS notifications
lead_indicators.channel: A tax or standards change moves demand within a quarter of taking effect

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when channel inventory is clean, unit volumes are growing in double digits, and metal prices are stable or falling; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a false dawn.

call.headline: Early up-cycle after two washed-out summers. Prefer appliance brand owners with clean channels and the lifestyle brands with pricing power; hold contract makers for the PLI volume story but do not pay for margins they will never have.
points: The GST cut on ACs, large TVs and dishwashers and a cleared channel have reset demand, so volumes should compound off a low base.
Copper and the rupee are still against the brand owners, so margin recovery lags volume recovery by a quarter or two.
Compressor and component localisation under the next PLI leg is a multi-year capex theme, not a quarterly one.
would_change: A third washed-out summer that refills the channel
A copper spike or a sharply weaker rupee that outruns price hikes
A reversal of the GST cut or a PLI target miss at a large contract maker

explainer.tell_a_friend: Consumer durables companies make or brand the things a household buys every few years on EMI: the air-conditioner, the fridge, the fan, the TV, the wedding gold. There are three kinds. Brand owners design and market the box and buy much of it from someone else; they live on summer heat, dealer shelf space and the copper price. Contract makers assemble phones and ACs for brands at a thin, fixed margin and win only on volume, which the PLI scheme has handed them since 2021. Lifestyle brands like a jeweller or a premium innerwear maker set their own price and keep the most. The cycle runs on two clocks: the summer and the festive quarter decide each year, while commodities, interest rates and policy set the longer swing. The 2022 and 2024 summers were booms, 2023 and 2025 were washouts, and then a GST cut before Diwali 2025 reset demand. Today the channel is clean and volumes are recovering, but copper is still high. Watch channel inventory after each season, gross margin, and the copper price.

glossary.def: Household goods that last years: appliances, electronics, furniture, jewellery and watches. Called white goods when they are large kitchen or laundry appliances.
A split or window air-conditioner for one room. The category that makes or breaks an Indian durables summer.
Assembling a product for a brand that sells it under its own name. EMS builds the brand's design; ODM designs it too.
Production-linked incentive: a government cash payment of roughly 4-6% on incremental sales of goods made in India, for phones, IT hardware, AC and LED components.
Global brands adding a second manufacturing base outside China, often India.
Sales minus raw materials and components, divided by sales. The commodity squeeze shows here first.
Finished goods sitting with distributors and dealers, already sold by the company but not yet to a household.
Pushing stock onto dealers at quarter-end to book sales. Shows up as rising receivable days.
Sales per rupee of plant and equipment. A contract maker turning assets 6 times a year can live on a 3% margin.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.
Money tied up in inventory and unpaid dealer bills, minus unpaid supplier bills. Swings with the season.
New plant spending divided by the yearly wear charge. Above 1 means building, near 1 means coasting.
The Bureau of Energy Efficiency's 1-to-5 star label on appliances. The scale is tightened every couple of years, so last year's 5-star becomes this year's 3-star.
An AC whose compressor runs at variable speed and uses less power. Now most of the market.
A rule that a product, including an imported one, must meet an Indian standard before it can be sold. Blocks cheap imports.
The global treaty phasing down HFC refrigerant gases. India's freeze starts in 2028, forcing new gases and compressors.
The rule that a brand must collect and recycle a set share of the e-waste from what it sold.
BIS certification of gold purity with a unique six-digit ID per piece, mandatory since 2021-23. Favours organised jewellers.
Jewellers borrow gold from banks instead of buying it, paying a lease rate; the cost sits in the interest line.
The weight of gold sold. When the price rallies, sales in rupees rise while grammage falls.
The goods and services tax rate band. ACs and large TVs moved from the 28% slab to 18% in 2025.
Big electronics chains like Croma, Reliance Digital and Vijay Sales, which negotiate hard on margins.
An instalment plan where the brand or financier absorbs the interest. Most big-ticket purchases in India use one.

explainer.one_liner: FMCG companies sell the small things every Indian household buys every week, a cigarette, a packet of tea, a bottle of cooking oil, a bag of atta, and make money by doing it a billion times through a million kirana shops.

doors.name: Tobacco cash machines
doors.sub: Cigarettes sold at a price the brand sets, under a heavy excise tax, with almost no competition from new brands
doors.blurb: A bet on the tax rate: volumes barely grow, but pricing power and cash flow are unmatched

doors.name: Branded staples and foods
doors.sub: Tea, salt, atta, spices, packaged foods and branded oil sold through distributors and kiranas at a modest margin
doors.blurb: A bet on distribution reach and on brands moving buyers from loose to packed

doors.name: Commodity processors and traders
doors.sub: Crush, refine, pack or trade edible oil, rice, sugar, seafood and pulses on a thin spread
doors.blurb: A bet on a commodity spread and on volume, not on a brand

doors.name: Farm-input sellers
doors.sub: Branded pesticides and fertiliser sold to farmers through dealers, filed under FMCG for their distribution model
doors.blurb: A bet on the monsoon, the sowing season and dealer credit

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the toll road the government taxes heavily but nobody can build a second one. Door two is the trusted kirana brand your mother asks for by name. Door three is the wholesale mandi trader who lives on the gap between buying and selling. Door four is the village seed-and-pesticide shop that watches the sky.
explainer.door_so_what: This industry label hides four very different businesses, so a tobacco name trades on tax news, a staples brand on volume growth, a processor on commodity spreads and a farm-input name on the monsoon; never compare their margins directly.

stations.name: Farm and import sourcing
stations.what: Tobacco leaf, tea, wheat, rice, oilseeds, imported palm and soybean oil and shrimp are bought from farms, auctions and ports
stations.who: Farmers, tea auctions, Indonesian and Malaysian palm exporters, AWL and PATANJALI as importers

stations.name: Processing and packing
stations.what: Leaf becomes cigarettes, crude oil becomes refined oil, wheat becomes atta, tea is blended and packed
stations.who: ITC, GODFRYPHLP, AWL, PATANJALI, TATACONSUM, and contract packers

stations.name: Brand and marketing
stations.what: Products get a name, a price point and ad money; most FMCG sells at fixed 'magic' price points
stations.who: ITC, TATACONSUM, PATANJALI, and the big MNCs in sister industries

stations.name: Distribution
stations.what: Super-stockists, distributors and salesmen push stock into kiranas, modern trade, e-commerce and quick-commerce dark stores
stations.who: Company-appointed distributors, Reliance Retail, DMart, Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart

stations.name: Kirana and household
stations.what: The household buys a sachet, a packet or a pouch, mostly with cash or UPI, mostly weekly
stations.who: A crore-plus kiranas, rural and urban households

kitchen.note: Cigarette plants cluster around Bengaluru, Kolkata and Saharanpur, edible-oil refineries sit at the Kandla, Haldia and Kakinada ports where the palm oil lands, and roughly a third of FMCG sales come from rural India. The cost line is the distributor's truck reaching a village shop.
kitchen.so_what: Because India imports most of its edible oil and the rest of the chain is domestic, the import station sets the commodity cost and the distribution station sets the share, and the listed names sit in the middle.

end_markets.name: Rural households
end_markets.buys: Sachets, small packs, loose-to-packed staples, beedi and cigarettes
end_markets.moves_with: Monsoon, farm prices, rural wages, government cash transfers

end_markets.name: Urban middle class
end_markets.buys: Premium tea, packaged foods, branded oil, cigarettes, ready-to-cook
end_markets.moves_with: Salaried incomes, food inflation, IT hiring

end_markets.name: Smokers
end_markets.buys: Cigarettes, mostly short and mid-length filter sticks
end_markets.moves_with: Excise and GST rates, the illicit-cigarette price gap

end_markets.name: Restaurants and caterers
end_markets.buys: Bulk oil, atta, rice, spices and tea
end_markets.moves_with: Eating-out frequency, wedding season

end_markets.name: Farmers
end_markets.buys: Pesticides, herbicides, fertiliser and seeds
end_markets.moves_with: Monsoon rainfall, crop prices, reservoir levels

end_markets.name: Export buyers
end_markets.buys: Basmati and non-basmati rice, shrimp, sugar, spices, leaf tobacco
end_markets.moves_with: Export bans and duties, US tariffs, global commodity prices

end_markets.name: Quick commerce and modern trade
end_markets.buys: Fast-moving packs and premium variants
end_markets.moves_with: Dark-store expansion, platform margins and discounting

explainer.end_markets_so_what: Rural volume is the swing factor in a normal year, so a good monsoon and firm crop prices are an FMCG volume signal two quarters before it shows in results.

lines.why: Palm oil, wheat, tea and leaf costs hit here first; FMCG prices at fixed price points, so a cost spike is absorbed by shrinking the pack before raising the price
The lever management pulls to defend share; cutting it flatters a quarter and loses share later
Tax is more than half the shelf price of a cigarette; any change resets volumes and margins in one budget
Branded names run negative working capital because distributors pay upfront; processors and farm-input sellers carry inventory and dealer credit for months
Plants are cheap relative to sales; depreciation is a small line for everyone except refiners
Asset-light brands turn assets many times a year; edible-oil refiners and cigarette plants are heavier but still modest
The big brands are debt-free; only commodity processors borrow, to fund inventory
ITC and other cash-rich names earn large treasury income that props up profit growth in slow years

pnl.analogy: An FMCG brand is a chaiwala at a busy railway platform: the tea and sugar cost little, the price is fixed at 'one cup', and the profit comes from how many cups he sells and how few customers walk to the next stall. When milk prices jump, he makes the cup a little smaller before he dares to raise the price.
pnl.so_what: Separate volume from price in every result: growth from price hikes with falling volumes is the beginning of trouble, growth from volume with flat prices is the start of a good run.

clock.is_cyclical: Mildly. Demand never collapses, but volume growth swings with rural incomes and food inflation, and margins swing with palm oil, wheat and crude, so the stocks go through long stretches of re-rating and de-rating.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: Lockdowns send households to pantry-loading staples and packaged foods; FMCG becomes the safe haven

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Palm oil hits a record after Indonesia's export ban, companies take record price hikes and shrink packs, and growth becomes all price

phases.name: Bust

phases.name: Bottom

clock.position_detail: GST cut helps, input costs rising again

timeline.what: A rural slowdown and a shadow-banking credit squeeze slow FMCG volumes to a crawl. The stocks still trade at premium multiples as a safe haven.
COVID-19 shuts kiranas briefly, then households stock up on staples and packaged foods. Cigarettes are hurt by lockdowns but recover; ITC is a laggard while food brands boom.
Russia's war and Indonesia's palm-oil export ban push input costs to records. Companies raise prices and shrink packs; rural buyers trade down to loose products and unbranded rivals.
Commodity prices fall and gross margins recover, but volumes lag. ITC becomes the market's favourite on stable cigarette taxes and a hotels demerger plan.
Rural demand starts recovering while urban demand slows. Tata Consumer buys Capital Foods and Organic India; quick commerce takes share in the big cities and distributors complain.

ITC Hotels is demerged, Adani exits Adani Wilmar which becomes AWL, and Reliance's Campa and value brands start a price war in staples and drinks. The GST rate cut in September moves most packaged foods to the lowest slab.

A new central excise on cigarettes replaces the old cess from February and lands as a steep tax increase, hitting ITC and Godfrey Phillips. Food and staples volumes recover on the GST cut and rural strength, but palm oil, crude and packaging costs are rising into the second half.

bottlenecks.name: Edible-oil import dependence
bottlenecks.why: India imports well over half its edible oil, mostly palm from Indonesia and Malaysia. A single export ban there reshapes Indian margins within weeks.

bottlenecks.name: Fixed price points
bottlenecks.why: Indian FMCG sells at 'magic' price points, so cost spikes are absorbed by shrinking packs, which buyers notice and resent.

bottlenecks.name: Tobacco tax risk
bottlenecks.why: The government sets most of a cigarette's price through tax, and a single budget or excise change can cut legal volumes by a big slice.

bottlenecks.name: Illicit cigarettes
bottlenecks.why: Smuggled and counterfeit cigarettes already take a large share; every tax hike widens the gap and grows the black market.

bottlenecks.name: Distributor and channel conflict
bottlenecks.why: Quick commerce and modern trade price below the kirana, and distributor associations push back against brands that favour them.

bottlenecks.name: Monsoon and food policy
bottlenecks.why: A failed monsoon cuts rural demand, and the government's export bans and stock limits can wipe out a trader's margin overnight.

bottlenecks.name: Unbranded and regional rivals
bottlenecks.why: Loose atta, local oil and regional tea brands undercut national brands whenever inflation squeezes budgets.

bottlenecks.name: Reliance's price war
bottlenecks.why: Reliance Consumer Products is using its retail reach to sell drinks and staples at sharply lower prices, forcing incumbents to respond.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: Import dependence and fixed price points set the margin ceiling; tobacco tax and food export policy are the surprise risks worth a news alert per company.

why.rivalry: Cigarettes are effectively a duopoly with a dominant leader; edible oil, rice and seafood have dozens of players selling the same product

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when volume growth is accelerating, rural is growing at least as fast as urban, and input costs are stable or falling; two of three means early recovery, one of three means a false dawn.

call.headline: Early volume recovery with a cost headwind. Prefer branded staples and foods names riding the GST cut and rural demand; stay cautious on tobacco until the new excise is absorbed in volumes.
points: The GST rate cut has handed packaged foods a price cut they did not pay for, and volumes are responding.
Rural demand has led urban for a year, which is the classic shape of an FMCG recovery.
The new cigarette excise is a steep increase, so legal volumes and margins at the tobacco names face a year of adjustment.
would_change: A failed monsoon that stalls rural demand
A palm-oil spike from an Indonesian export curb or a sharply weaker rupee
A deeper Reliance price war that forces incumbents to cut prices

explainer.tell_a_friend: FMCG companies sell the small things you buy every week: cigarettes, tea, cooking oil, atta, salt. In India this label hides four businesses. Cigarette makers like ITC are cash machines because the law bans new brands from advertising, but the government sets most of the price through tax. Branded staples sellers like Tata Consumer earn a modest margin by reaching a million kirana shops. Edible-oil refiners and rice traders live on a thin commodity spread. And a few pesticide sellers sit here because they sell through dealers. The cycle is gentle but real: in 2022 palm oil and wheat costs spiked, companies raised prices and shrank packs, and rural buyers stopped buying. Margins rebuilt in 2024 and 2025, and the September 2025 GST cut is now lifting volumes. The new cigarette excise from 2026 is a headwind for ITC. Watch volume growth, the monsoon and palm-oil prices.

glossary.def: Fast-moving consumer goods: cheap, everyday products bought often, such as food, tea, soap and cigarettes.
The neighbourhood general store. India has more than 1 crore of them and they still sell most FMCG.
A fixed retail price like ₹5 or ₹10 that buyers expect; companies change the pack size instead of the price.
Keeping the price the same while putting less product in the pack.
Growth in the quantity sold, after removing the effect of price hikes.
Sales minus raw materials and packaging, divided by sales.
Operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, divided by sales.
Ad spend plus trade schemes and discounts given to push a brand; usually 5-12% of sales.
Distributors pay the company before the company pays its suppliers, so the business runs on other people's money.
Middlemen who buy from the company and supply kiranas in a territory, earning a few per cent.
Supermarket and hypermarket chains like DMart and Reliance Smart.
Grocery delivered within 10-30 minutes from dark stores: Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto.
A central tax per stick, set by length; replaced the GST compensation cess from February 2026.
The 2003 tobacco law banning tobacco advertising and mandating health warnings.
Smuggled or counterfeit cigarettes that pay no tax; estimated at about a quarter of the market.
The cheapest edible oil, imported mostly from Indonesia and Malaysia; also a raw material for soaps and snacks.
The shift from unbranded staples weighed out at the shop to sealed, branded packs.
A proposed FSSAI rule to print warnings for high sugar, salt or fat on the front of food packs.
The rural jobs guarantee scheme; its payouts are a direct source of rural cash.
Return on capital employed: operating profit divided by the money invested in the business.
The goods and services tax rate band. Most packaged foods moved to the 5% slab in September 2025.
The monsoon-sown crop season from June to October; its success sets rural incomes for the year.

explainer.one_liner: Food and beverage companies turn milk, wheat, sugar, cocoa, coffee, barley and molasses into the Maggi, the biscuit, the Pepsi, the beer, the whisky and the pizza that Indians eat and drink, and the best of them charge far more for the brand than for the ingredients.

doors.blurb: A bet on brand power, distribution reach and soft commodity prices

doors.sub: Sugar and ethanol mills, rice millers and instant-coffee makers selling in bulk or under thin-margin brands
doors.blurb: A bet on a crop, a government price and an export rule

explainer.door_analogy: Door one is the Parle-G of your childhood: the same packet, bought forever. Door two is the theka and the cold-drink fridge, where the state taxman and the weather decide the year. Door three is the mall food court that lives on footfall. Door four is the sugar mill down the road, waiting for the cane price and the export notice.
explainer.door_so_what: A packaged food brand trades on volume and margin stability, a liquor name on premiumisation and state taxes, a restaurant chain on same-store sales and a processor on a government-set price, so read the door before you read the multiple.

kitchen.note: Sugar mills cluster in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka, dairies in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Punjab, and every state runs its own liquor market with its own tax, price and route to the shop. Moving a bottle of whisky across a state border is a regulatory event, not a logistics one.
kitchen.so_what: The farm sets the cost and the state sets the price for a large chunk of this industry, so the listed brands earn their keep only where they can price above both.

pnl.analogy: A packaged food brand is the Bikaneri bhujia seller whose name commands a premium over the same snack from a nameless shop. A restaurant chain is the dhaba on the highway: the food cost is small, the rent and the staff are the whole story, and a quiet month hurts.
pnl.so_what: Read gross margin for food brands, state-level price approvals for liquor, and same-store sales for restaurants; each door has one number that tells you most of the quarter.

clock.is_cyclical: Mildly for packaged food, more so for drinks and restaurants. Packaged food swings with commodity costs and rural demand, drinks with the summer and state taxes, and restaurants with urban discretionary spending; sugar runs on its own cane-and-policy cycle.

phases.what: Wheat, milk, palm oil and barley costs hit records; companies take big price hikes and restaurant stocks trade at rich multiples

phases.name: Bust

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: Input costs ease, the GST cut lands on packaged food, and restaurant chains stabilise on delivery and value menus

clock.position_detail: GST cut, premium drinks strong, restaurants lagging

timeline.what: A consumption slowdown hits biscuits and snacks at the bottom of the pyramid. Restaurant chains and premium liquor are still growing fast.
COVID-19 shuts restaurants and liquor shops. When liquor shops reopen, queues stretch for kilometres; households stock up on noodles and biscuits.

Reopening brings back dine-in and drinking; Jubilant and Devyani boom on delivery and expansion, Varun Beverages scales across India and Africa. Then wheat, milk and barley costs spike and companies raise prices hard.

Restaurant same-store sales turn negative as urban diners pull back. Food inflation slows volumes. Sugar mills pivot to ethanol, Nestle and Britannia hold margins while volumes lag, and premium whisky keeps growing.

Maharashtra raises liquor excise sharply. The India-UK trade deal halves the duty on Scotch over time. The September GST cut moves most packaged foods to the lowest slab and an early monsoon dampens the summer for drinks.

Packaged food volumes recover on the GST cut and rural demand, Hatsun targets a big growth leg, and premium spirits keep compounding. Cocoa and coffee costs are easing from records, sugar mills crush early before Diwali, and restaurant chains are recovering slowly.

explainer.dials_so_what: If you track only two dials, track food inflation for the food brands and the summer for the drinks makers; state excise is the third for anyone holding liquor.

bottlenecks.name: State-by-state liquor rules
bottlenecks.why: Every state sets its own excise, price and route to market, and some ban alcohol outright. A new government or a budget can reset a market overnight.

bottlenecks.name: Milk and farm cost swings
bottlenecks.why: Milk, wheat and sugar prices follow the monsoon and government support prices, and brands cannot fully hedge them.

bottlenecks.name: Restaurant rent and delivery cuts
bottlenecks.why: Rent and delivery-app commissions take a large share of a restaurant's sales, and both keep rising.

bottlenecks.name: Sugar and ethanol policy
bottlenecks.why: The government sets cane prices, sugar export quotas, the minimum sale price and the ethanol price; mill profits are a policy output.

bottlenecks.name: Weather risk for drinks
bottlenecks.why: A rainy April or an early monsoon can cut a quarter of the summer's volume for soft drinks, beer and ice cream.

bottlenecks.name: Advertising ban on liquor
bottlenecks.why: Alcohol cannot be advertised directly, which protects incumbents but makes launching a new brand slow.

bottlenecks.name: Health and sugar scrutiny
bottlenecks.why: FSSAI labelling rules, sugar taxes and influencer criticism of health drinks put pressure on high-sugar products.

bottlenecks.name: Slow state payments
bottlenecks.why: State beverage corporations in states like Tamil Nadu and Telangana pay liquor makers late, tying up cash.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: State liquor rules and farm cost swings set the ceiling on margins; the weather and policy notices are the surprise risks worth a news alert per company.

why.rivalry: Food categories have one or two dominant brands each; restaurants fight dozens of chains and local kitchens, and sugar mills sell a commodity
why.supplier: Milk and wheat come from millions of farmers with little pricing power; restaurant landlords, delivery apps and the cane price set by government squeeze the rest
why.buyer: A shopper buying Maggi does not negotiate; restaurant diners switch on a coupon and sugar buyers on a paisa
why.entrants: Distribution and trust take decades to build in packaged food; a new pizza brand or cloud kitchen can open in months
why.substitutes: Home cooking and local snacks substitute everywhere; cooking at home is the restaurant's biggest rival

forces.so_what: Packaged food brands keep the most because trust and distribution are their moat, drinks makers keep a good share where states let them price, and restaurant chains and processors keep the least because rent, cane prices and rivals take it.
