lead_indicators.channel: Land bought today is a launch in a year and a margin for five

rule.text: The industry is in an up-cycle when unit sales are rising, unsold inventory is falling and home-loan rates are steady or falling; two of three means a plateau, one of three means a downturn is starting.

call.headline: A late-cycle plateau. Prefer annuity owners and net-cash developers with land bought cheap over developers that borrowed to buy land at the top.
points: Rate cuts help, but mid-income affordability, not money, is now the constraint.
Luxury and branded developers keep taking share from smaller rivals, so volumes hold better for listed names than for the market.
Mall and office rents are still rising, which makes annuity income the steadier part of the sector.
would_change: Unit sales turning up again with stable prices, which would restart the cycle
A sharp stock-market fall, which would hit luxury demand first
Rising rates or a funding squeeze, which would hit leveraged developers

explainer.tell_a_friend: Real estate developers sell flats years before they are built, collect the buyers' money in stages, and use it to build. The real top line is pre-sales, the value of flats sold this quarter, not reported revenue, which only appears at handover. After a long bust from 2013 to 2019, when stalled projects and a funding crunch killed many developers, RERA pushed buyers towards trusted listed names, and from 2021 to 2024 they had a record run led by luxury homes in Gurugram, Mumbai and Bengaluru. Now prices have run ahead of salaries, unit sales are flat and unsold inventory is creeping up in places, even as rates fall. Some developers also own malls and offices, which earn steady rising rent, and those are the calmer part of the sector. Watch pre-sales volume, unsold inventory, net debt and home-loan rates.

glossary.def: The value of flats booked by buyers in a period. Not revenue yet, but the best read of demand.
Cash actually received from buyers, in instalments linked to construction progress.
Under Indian accounting rules, developers book revenue and profit only when a project is handed over, often 3-5 years after the sale.
The Real Estate Regulation Act of 2016: every project registers with a state authority, 70% of buyer money sits in escrow, and delays are penalised.
A project bank account that can only be spent on that project's land and construction.
The landowner contributes land and gets a share of flats or revenue instead of cash, so the developer needs less money upfront.
Flats launched but not sold, often expressed as months of sales at the current pace.
Recurring rent from malls, offices and data centres the developer keeps.
Yearly rent divided by the property's value; a lower cap rate means a higher valuation.
Floor space index: how many square feet you may build per square foot of land, set by the city.
The minimum value a state assigns to property for stamp duty; sales cannot be registered below it.
A state tax on property purchases, usually 5-7% of value plus registration.
An in-house technology or back-office hub of a foreign company, now the largest office tenant in India.
Borrowings minus cash. Developers with net cash survive downturns.
Infrastructure investment trust: a listed trust that owns roads or power lines and pays out most of its cash.
Real estate investment trust: a listed trust that owns rented offices or malls and pays out at least 90% of its cash.

explainer.one_liner: REITs and InvITs are listed trusts that own finished, rent-paying assets such as office parks, malls, power lines, toll roads and solar farms, and hand almost all the cash they collect to unitholders every quarter, so you can own a slice of a Bengaluru tech park the way you own a share.

doors.name: Office REITs
doors.sub: Own Grade-A tech parks leased to global companies on long leases with rent steps every few years
doors.blurb: A bet on global companies keeping and growing their Indian offices, and on bond yields falling

doors.name: Retail REIT
doors.sub: Owns city malls; earns fixed rent plus a share of each store's sales
doors.blurb: A bet on urban shopping and on the mall winning against e-commerce and quick commerce

doors.name: Infrastructure InvITs
doors.sub: Own power lines, roads and solar farms paid by regulated tariffs, annuities or tolls
doors.blurb: A bet on a bond-like payout with a fixed end date, so the price trades mostly against the government bond

doors.name: Small and medium REITs
doors.sub: Own a single small office or building, sold to investors through fractional-ownership platforms
doors.blurb: A bet on one building and one or two tenants, with thin trading

explainer.door_analogy: An office REIT is a landlord of a huge tech campus, the retail REIT is the landlord of a mall who also takes a cut of every shop's till, an InvIT owns the toll booths and power lines on a highway, and a small REIT is a group of friends who jointly bought one shop to rent out.
explainer.door_so_what: Office and retail REITs can grow their payout by raising rent and filling space, while most InvITs pay out a fixed stream that shrinks to zero at the end of a concession, so the same yield means very different things.

stations.what: A developer or private-equity sponsor builds and leases up the park, mall, road or line
stations.who: Blackstone, Brookfield, K Raheja, Embassy, Sattva, KKR and power developers

stations.who: KRT, EMBASSY, MINDSPACE, BIRET, NXST, INDIGRID and the other trusts' managers

stations.name: Distribution
stations.what: At least nine-tenths of distributable cash is paid out each quarter as dividend, interest and debt repayment
stations.who: The trusts, to mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and retail

stations.name: Growth by acquisition
stations.what: The trust buys new assets from its sponsor or the market, using debt and fresh units
stations.who: Sponsors' pipelines, third-party sellers, lenders

kitchen.rival: The government bond yield, the benchmark every payout competes with
kitchen.note: Office REIT assets cluster in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and the NCR, mostly in tech parks that grew up around IT services firms. Global private-equity firms built most of these assets and still sponsor most of the listed trusts.
kitchen.so_what: The listed trusts do one job, operate and pay out, so their value is set by rent growth and the bond yield, while growth comes from what the sponsor is willing to sell into them.

pnl.analogy: A REIT is a building society that collects rent from tenants, pays the watchman and the bank loan, and shares what is left among the flat owners every three months. The share grows only if rents rise, empty flats fill or the loan gets cheaper.
pnl.so_what: Value office and retail REITs on distribution growth plus occupancy, and InvITs on yield against the bond and the years left on each concession.

clock.is_cyclical: Office REITs follow the office leasing cycle and the interest-rate cycle; InvITs follow interest rates almost alone. Both behave more like bonds with a growth kicker than like stocks.

phases.name: Boom
phases.what: The first office REIT lists to strong demand, InvITs and IT hiring both expand

phases.name: Peak
phases.what: Units hit highs just as Covid empties offices

phases.name: Bust
phases.what: Work from home, US tech layoffs and rising rates push vacancies up and unit prices down by a fifth or more

phases.name: Bottom
phases.what: GCC leasing restarts, rate hikes end, units trade well below asset values

clock.position_detail: leasing strong, rates falling

timeline.what: Embassy lists India's first REIT, backed by Blackstone. InvITs for power lines and roads are already trading.
Covid sends everyone home. Mindspace and Brookfield still list, but vacancy rises and investors worry offices are finished.

Rate hikes and US tech layoffs keep units under pressure. SEZ campuses are hard to fill because domestic tenants cannot use them easily. A tax change makes part of the payout taxable. Nexus Select lists as the first mall REIT.
Global capability centres lead record office leasing. SEBI creates small and medium REITs for single buildings. Vacancy starts falling.
Knowledge Realty Trust lists as the largest office REIT. The RBI cuts rates, SEZ rules are eased so vacant floors can go to domestic tenants, and SEBI moves to treat REITs as equity for mutual funds.
Occupancy keeps climbing, rents on renewal step up, and lower borrowing costs flow into payouts. The equity classification widens the buyer base; index inclusion is the next question.

bottlenecks.name: Sponsor concentration
bottlenecks.why: A handful of global private-equity sponsors own most listed trusts and decide which assets get sold in and at what price.

bottlenecks.name: SEZ vacancy
bottlenecks.why: Many tech parks sit in special economic zones that domestic tenants could not easily use; rules eased in 2025, but older vacant blocks take time to fill.

bottlenecks.name: Lease expiry clusters
bottlenecks.why: Many leases signed in the late-2010s boom come up together; renewals are a chance to raise rent or a risk of losing a tenant.

bottlenecks.name: Concession end dates
bottlenecks.why: A road or power InvIT's asset goes back to the government at the end of its concession, so part of every payout is a return of capital.

bottlenecks.name: Thin retail ownership and liquidity
bottlenecks.why: Most units sit with institutions, and small REITs trade rarely, so prices can swing on small flows.

bottlenecks.name: Tax rule changes
bottlenecks.why: The 2023 change that taxed debt-repayment payouts showed how quickly after-tax yields can move.

explainer.bottlenecks_so_what: Sponsor concentration and concession end dates never go away; lease expiries and tax changes are the quarter-to-quarter surprises.

rule.text: The sector is in an up-cycle when office vacancy is falling, bond yields are falling and renewals reprice above old rents; two of three means a steady payout, one of three means prices drift down.

call.headline: A healthy up-cycle with both legs working. Prefer office REITs with spare land to build on and low SEZ exposure; treat InvITs as bond substitutes that are now fairly priced after the rate cuts.
points: Global capability centres keep leasing record space, which pushes up occupancy and renewal rents.
Lower borrowing costs feed directly into distributions at each refinancing.
Equity classification for mutual funds widens the buyer base and could bring index inclusion.

explainer.tell_a_friend: A REIT is a listed trust that owns rented buildings, like a big Bengaluru tech park or a city mall, and must pay out almost all the cash it collects every quarter. An InvIT does the same with power lines, toll roads and solar farms. You buy units on the exchange and get a payout like rent. Office REITs grow their payout when they fill empty floors and raise rents at renewal; InvITs mostly pay a fixed stream that ends when the concession ends, so they behave like bonds. After Covid and rate hikes hurt them between 2021 and 2023, office REITs are now in a good patch: foreign companies are leasing record space for their India centres, rates have fallen, and SEBI has let mutual funds treat REITs as equity. Watch the bond yield, office vacancy and rent on renewals.

glossary.def: Real estate investment trust: a listed trust owning rent-paying property that must distribute at least 90% of its distributable cash.
Infrastructure investment trust: the same structure for roads, power lines, solar farms and pipelines.
The share of a REIT or InvIT that investors buy on the exchange.
Net distributable cash flow: the cash left after costs, interest and reserves, at least 90% of which must be paid out.
The cash paid per unit, made up of dividend, interest and repayment of debt, each taxed differently.
Rent and other property income minus the costs of running the property.
The share of leasable area under signed leases, including leases not yet started.
The change in rent when an old lease is renewed or re-let, usually as a percentage.
Weighted average lease expiry: the average years left on leases, weighted by rent.
Independent valuers' estimate of the assets, minus debt, per unit.
The developer or private-equity firm that set up the trust and usually still holds a big stake and an asset pipeline.
Modern office buildings with large floors, power backup and global-standard facilities that multinational tenants require.
Special economic zone: an area with export tax benefits where many tech parks were built; tenants face usage restrictions.
An in-house technology or back-office hub of a foreign company, now the biggest office tenant in India.
The fixed period, often 20-30 years, for which a road or power asset earns before it returns to the government.
Mall rent linked to a store's sales, on top of fixed rent.
A SEBI category from 2024 for trusts owning assets worth ₹50-500 crore, often a single building.
The distribution yield minus the 10-year government bond yield; the extra pay for owning units.
